sens: To undergo compression, a physical crushing
To be flattened, pressed into a fixed position
To be mistreated, subjected to violent pressure
H4600.detail:
1. The word primarily describes the action of crushing or compressing something. In Leviticus 22:24, it refers to the testicles of an animal that have been crushed, bruised, or mutilated: the law prohibited offering as a sacrifice an animal that was thus damaged. It is the physical image of compression.
2. To be crushed can also mean to be pressed down, flattened, held in place by pressure. In 1 Samuel 26:7, Saul's spear is thrust into the ground at his bedside: it is fixed there by its weight and the pressure that immobilizes it.
3. The word takes on a dimension of violence and violation when it describes how something or someone is mistreated, crushed by force. In Ezekiel 23:3, the breasts of young women have been "pressed": this evokes sexual brutality, a domination imposed by violence.
H4600.origine: The Hebrew verb ma'akh comes from a root that expresses the idea of pressure, of compression. Its fundamental meaning is physical: to press, to crush under weight or force. The family of this word includes the general idea of violent manipulation or mistreatment. In biblical Hebrew, this verb appears in different forms that nuance the action: in the Qal (simple form) it means "to be crushed," in the Pual (passive form) "to be manipulated or pressed."
H4600.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Leviticus 22:24, it relates to the physical defects of a sacrificial animal: any animal whose testicles have been crushed was declared unfit for sacrifice. In 1 Samuel 26:7, it describes Saul's spear thrust into the ground. In Ezekiel 23:3, it designates the sexual assault suffered by young women in Egypt, an act of violence and domination. Through these three uses, the word retains its fundamental meaning of compression or crushing, but applied to different contexts: mutilated animal, fixed object, or person victimized by violence.
H4600.portee: This word reminds us that the Mosaic law paid careful attention to the quality of offerings and the protection of the dignity of the sacrifice. It also shows how the Bible does not hide the violence suffered by the most vulnerable, particularly women, giving their suffering a place in the Word of God.

sens: Son of Nahor and his concubine Reumah
H4601G.detail: Maaca is a character in the Old Testament mentioned only once in Genesis. He is one of the sons that Nahor had with his concubine Reumah, alongside Tebah, Gaham, and Tahash. This name appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Abraham, particularly among the descendants of his brother Nahor (Genesis 22:24).
H4601G.origine: The name Maaca means "oppression" in Hebrew. It is formed from a root that evokes the idea of pressing, burdening, or oppressing. This name belongs to the proper names attested in the patriarchal genealogies of Genesis.
H4601G.emploi: Maaca appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 22:24, where he is listed among the children of Nahor born to his concubine Reumah. He is part of the genealogies that establish the familial ties between Abraham and the peoples of the Levant, thus allowing readers to place Nahor and his descendants in the patriarchal history.

sens: Small Aramean kingdom located in northern Syria, ally of Ammon
H4601H.detail: 1. Maaca is a small Aramean (Syrian) state in the north, which the Ammonites hire as mercenaries to fight King David. The text of 1 Chronicles 19:6 shows that Hanun, son of Ammon, sends 1,000 talents of silver to pay for chariots and horsemen provided by Maaca and other Syrian kingdoms. This is an example of these small regional powers that rented their soldiers to neighboring kingdoms.
H4601H.origine: The name Maaca means "oppression" in Hebrew. It is an Aramean (Syrian) kingdom, one of the many small states that existed in northern Syria around the time of King David (circa the 10th century BC). This territory was a minor but active political player in regional conflicts.
H4601H.emploi: Maaca appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 19:6, where it is listed among the mercenary allies hired by the Ammonites to fight David. It is mentioned alongside other Syrian kingdoms like Zobah. The Bible designates it as a military power capable of providing chariots and horsemen for war.
H4601H.portee: This passage reminds the reader that the kingdoms of the ancient Near East, even the smallest, had strategic importance and that military alliances were a common reality of the time. It is also a sign of the scope of David's power, as even external mercenary allies were not enough to stop David.

sens: Wife of David, mother of Prince Absalom
Daughter of King Talmai of Geshur
H4601I.detail: Maaca is a woman of the royal court during the time of King David. She is first identified as the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, a small kingdom located east of the Jordan. She marries David and becomes the mother of Absalom, one of the king's most important sons (2 Samuel 3:3). Her marriage alliance with David seals a diplomatic relationship between Israel and the small nation of Geshur, which was a common practice among ancient kings to strengthen peace.
H4601I.origine: The name Maaca literally means "oppression" in Hebrew. It likely reflects a historical or symbolic reality of the context of the time, although the Bible does not explain it in detail. What we know about Maaca is related to her role as the mother of Absalom and her royal Geshurite lineage, which gave her a high status at David's court.
H4601I.emploi: Maaca appears only twice in the Bible, always mentioned in connection with her royal lineage and her role as a mother. In 2 Samuel 3:3 and 1 Chronicles 3:2, she is presented as the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, and as the mother of Absalom. These two royal passages establish her genealogy in the context of the wives and sons of King David, highlighting her dynastic importance. She embodies a political-family alliance that united Israel and Geshur during the time of the united monarchy.

sens: Woman of the tribe of Judah, wife of King Rehoboam
Mother of King Abijah of Judah
Queen exercising political and religious influence at court
H4601K.detail: Maaca is a woman of the people of Judah, daughter of Absalom (the rebellious son of King David), who became the wife of King Rehoboam. She played an important role at the royal court: Rehoboam loved her more than all his other wives and concubines (2 Chronicles 11:21), and she bore several sons, including Abijah, whom Rehoboam made chief among his brothers to make him his successor (2 Chronicles 11:22). Her religious influence is evident in 1 Kings 15:13, where King Asa, her grandson, had to remove her title of queen mother because she had made an idol for Ashtoreth, the pagan goddess; he destroyed the idol at the brook Kidron. Maaca thus represents a powerful woman who, despite her high position at court, retained idolatrous practices.
H4601K.origine: The Hebrew name Maaca (מַעֲכָה) literally means "oppression" or "compression." Her father was Absalom, the son of David known for his rebellion against his father and his dramatic death. Through her mother, she was linked to the royal house of David, which allowed her to rise to the rank of queen and exercise decisive influence over the royal succession.
H4601K.emploi: Maaca appears 7 times in the biblical texts, especially in the accounts of the kings of Judah. She is first mentioned in 1 Kings 15:2 and 15:10 as the mother of King Abijah, daughter of Absalom. The details of her life as a queen and her influence at court are reported in 2 Chronicles 11:20-22: Rehoboam, who had several wives, chose her among them and preferred her to all the others, and he made her son Abijah the heir to the throne. Her problematic religious role appears in 1 Kings 15:13 and 2 Chronicles 15:16, where she is seen stripped of her dignity as queen mother because of her impious idol.
H4601K.portee: Maaca shows how power and influence at court were not a guarantee of faithfulness to God. Although married to a king and mother of a king, she clung to pagan worship and had to be corrected by her descendants. Her story teaches that even the highest positions in human hierarchy remain subject to divine judgment on idolatry.

sens: Woman of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
Concubine of Caleb, son of Hezron
Mother of Sheber, Tirchanah, Shaph, and Sheva
H4601L.detail: Maaca is a woman of the tribe of Judah who lived during the divided monarchy (the kingdoms of Israel and Judah separated). She was the concubine of Caleb, son of Hezron, meaning a secondary wife of the family leader, which was a common practice in ancient Israel. She bore four sons: Sheber, Tirchanah, Shaph, and Sheva, who carried their father's name and formed a branch of Caleb's descendants.
H4601L.origine: The name Maaca means "oppression" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that evokes crushing or compression. This name, although dark in its literal sense, was borne by several women in the genealogy of Israel. Maaca is mentioned only in the genealogical lists of the first book of Chronicles, which enumerate the descendants of the important tribes and families of Judah.
H4601L.emploi: Maaca appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:48, in a detailed genealogy of Caleb's descendants. She is simply presented as the concubine who bore four sons to the family leader. This brief mention is part of the systematic recording of generations that connect the ancestors of the people of Judah to the following generations. Her unique appearance emphasizes that even the least prominent women in genealogical lists had a defined place in the history of the chosen people.

sens: Woman of the tribe of Manasseh, wife of Makir
H4601M.detail: Maaca is a woman of the tribe of Manasseh mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Manasseh. She was the daughter of Ir, sister of Shuppim and Huppim (1 Chronicles 7:15). She married Makir and bore him at least two sons: Peresh and Sheresh (1 Chronicles 7:16). Her name means "oppression" in Hebrew.
H4601M.origine: The name Maaca comes from Hebrew and literally means "oppression." It is formed from a root that evokes the idea of pressing or overwhelming. This name, like many Hebrew names, likely reflected a circumstance or reality at the time of the child's birth.
H4601M.emploi: Maaca is mentioned twice in the Bible, both in the context of the genealogy of the tribe of Manasseh in 1 Chronicles 7. She first appears as the sister of Shuppim and Huppim (1 Chronicles 7:15), and immediately afterward as the wife of Makir who bore sons. These verses are part of the genealogical record that lists the descendants of Manasseh and establishes the important family lines for the people of Israel. Her role is that of a mother and wife in the continuity of the tribe.

sens: Woman of the tribe of Benjamin during the united monarchy
Wife of Abiel and mother of ten sons
Ancestor of the Saul royal family
H4601N.detail:
1. Maaca is a woman of the tribe of Benjamin who lived during the time when Israel was united under one king. She appears in the genealogical record of 1 Chronicles 8:29.
2. She is the wife of Abiel and becomes the mother of many children: Kish, Ner, Abdon, Zur, Baal, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zecher, and Mikloth. She is a woman with a significant role in her lineage.
3. Through her son Kish, she is the ancestor of King Saul, the first king of Israel. Her descendants play a key role in the history of Israel.
H4601N.origine: The name Maaca means "oppression" in Hebrew. It expresses an idea of weight, burden, or tribulation — a well-known reality in ancient Israel, where women had to endure family and social trials. The name carries within it the awareness of life's difficulties while designating a woman who founded an important lineage.
H4601N.emploi: Maaca appears twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles: first in 8:29, then in 9:35, in practically identical passages that recap the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. These two occurrences do not describe events but establish her place in the genealogical tree of Abiel and introduce her ten sons. She is important not for her reported actions but for her position as a wife and mother in the succession that will lead to King Saul.

sens: Father of Hanan, one of David's mighty warriors
H4601O.detail: Maaca is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the divided monarchy in Israel and Judah. He is the father of Hanan, who is among the renowned and mighty warriors of King David (1 Chronicles 11:43). His existence is known to us only through this genealogy of the elite fighters surrounding the king.
H4601O.origine: The name Maaca means "oppression" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that denotes pressure or compression. Like many Hebrew names, it reflects either a circumstance of birth or an expected quality or a prayer from the father.
H4601O.emploi: Maaca appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 11:43. He is mentioned as the father of Hanan in the list of David's mighty warriors — these chosen men renowned for their strength and courage in battle who formed the royal military elite. No additional details about his life or deeds are provided by the biblical text.

sens: A man from the time of the divided monarchy
Father of the tribal prince Schephathia
Name meaning "oppression"
H4601P.detail: Maaca is a man from the people of Simeon living during the time of King David. He is the father of Schephathia, who is designated as prince (chief) of the tribe of Simeon during David's reign, according to the census of tribal leaders (1 Chronicles 27:16). His name carries the meaning "oppression" in Hebrew.
H4601P.origine: The Hebrew name Maaca (מַעֲכָה) literally means "oppression" or "pressure." It comes from a root that evokes the idea of weighing down someone, compressing, or crushing. This name was borne in the families of Israel and likely recalled a difficult reality of its familial or national context at the time.
H4601P.emploi: Maaca appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:16, where he is presented as the father of Schephathia. The latter is mentioned among the leaders of the twelve tribes of Israel during David's time. This administrative passage lists the tribal and military leaders of the kingdom. Maaca himself does not perform any notable deeds: he is only identified by his paternity, which was common in biblical genealogies.

sens: Father of King Achish of Gath
H4601Q.detail: Maaca is the father of Achish, king of the Philistine city of Gath during the reign of Solomon. He appears in the Bible only for this lineage: in 1 Kings 2:39, two servants of the Judean Shimei flee to Achish "son of Maaca" to seek refuge.
H4601Q.origine: The name Maaca literally means "oppression" in Hebrew (formed from the root that denotes an action of crushing or pressing). It is a theophoric name, characteristic of royal Philistine names from the Iron Age, although it is also found in Jewish genealogies. This character and his son Achish embody the regional powers with which Israel and Judah must contend at the time of the transition between David and Solomon.
H4601Q.emploi: Maaca is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 2:39. He is identified solely as the father of King Achish of Gath, one of the five main city-states of the Philistines. This context shows a moment of relative political stability where rival kingdoms—Gath and Judah—maintain sufficiently peaceful relations for Judean servants to find asylum there.

sens: Small kingdom or vassal state in Southwest Asia, bordering Israel
People or ethnic group established in this territory
Mercenary ally of the Ammonites against Israel
H4601R.detail:
1. Maaca is a small state located in the mountainous region east of the Jordan, near the Ammonite lands. Its existence was known at the time of the wars of King David (around 1000 BCE), and it had a king governing its own people. The first mention in 2 Samuel 10:6 refers to it as one of the powers that the Ammonites hire as mercenaries.

2. The inhabitants of Maaca, called Maacathites, formed a distinct population in this region of Southwest Asia. Joshua 13:13 mentions them as a group that the Israelites did not completely conquer during their settlement in the promised land.

3. During the conflict between David and the Ammonites, the king of Maaca and his troops fight alongside the Ammonites: they position themselves for battle at the entrance of the gate (2 Samuel 10:8) and camp before Medeba (1 Chronicles 19:7), serving as auxiliary forces in this war.
H4601R.origine: The name Maaca means "oppression" in Hebrew. This etymology may reflect the political or military nature of this small state with disputed borders in ancient Southwest Asia.
H4601R.emploi: Maaca is mentioned four times in the Bible, exclusively in military and political contexts. It appears mainly during David's wars against the Ammonites (circa 1000 BCE), in two parallel passages of 2 Samuel 10 and 1 Chronicles 19. The king of Maaca and his warriors are among the mercenary allies that the sons of Ammon hire against Israel. Maaca also exists at the time of the conquest, as Joshua 13:13 mentions it as a territory that the Geshurites and the Maacathites retained without being fully subdued by Israel. Thus, it is a small independent or semi-independent kingdom, strategically located on the margins of the promised land.

sens: people of Transjordan
inhabitant or warrior of the kingdom of Maacah
H4602.detail:
1. The Maacathites are a people established in Transjordan, beyond the Jordan, in the mountainous regions. They occupy the territory around Maacah, towards Hermon and Bashan (Joshua 13:11). This border region remained partially independent for a long time, as the Israelites never completely conquered them (Joshua 13:13).
2. The term also refers to an individual from this people or belonging to it. Elephalet, a warrior in King David's army, is described as "son of a Maacathite" (2 Samuel 23:34), just as Jaazania is called "son of the Maacathite" (2 Kings 25:23) — these men retained this ethnic identity even while serving the kings of Israel and Judah.
H4602.origine: The name comes from Maacah (H4601), which literally means "she has pressed" or "pressure," probably an image of strength or territorial tightening. The Maacathites are thus the descendants or inhabitants of this nation-state of Maacah, forming a distinct ethnic group in Transjordan.
H4602.emploi: The term appears 8 times in the Bible, always in a geopolitical or military context. During the conquest of Canaan, Maacah was a small independent power alongside Geshur, controlling the northern Transjordan (Deuteronomy 3:14; Joshua 12:5, 13:11). The Maacathites were never fully subjugated to Israel and maintained their autonomy (Joshua 13:13). Subsequently, Maacathite warriors are found in the service of the Israelite and Judean kings, or playing important political roles after the Babylonian exile (2 Samuel 23:34; 2 Kings 25:23).

sens: Commit infidelity, betray a commitment or alliance
Violate an obligation to God, transgress His commandments
Betray someone's trust, act disloyally towards them
Profane a consecrated or sacred thing
H4603.detail:
1. To be unfaithful means to break a commitment one has made. The word evokes one who "turns their back" on a promise, a contract, or a relationship. When a woman "has been unfaithful to her husband" (Numbers 5:27), she has betrayed the marriage covenant. Similarly, Israel "sinned against the Lord" (2 Chronicles 30:7) by worshiping other gods despite the covenant made.

2. It also refers to transgressing God's commandments, disobeying Him voluntarily or involuntarily. One who "commits infidelity" against the "consecrated things" (Leviticus 5:15) profanes what is reserved for God. King Uzziah "sinned against the Lord" by burning incense himself in the temple (2 Chronicles 26:16), an action forbidden to non-priests.

3. It is to betray someone, to act disloyally towards them. Joshua reassures the tribes of the East: "You have not committed this infidelity against the Lord" (Joshua 22:31), meaning you have not betrayed Him through rebellion.

4. The word can also refer to the profanation of what is holy and set apart. One who "sins" against the consecrated things violates a serious prohibition regarding the domain of God.
H4603.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of "turning the back," of "crossing a boundary." It is related to the noun מַעַל (transgression, betrayal). The basic image is that of crossing a boundary: one exceeds the limit that was to be respected. The word is used for any breach of commitment — towards a man, towards a covenant, towards God — and for the violation of the sacred domain.
H4603.emploi: This verb appears 35 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in legal books (Leviticus, Numbers), history (1-2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah), and the prophets (Ezekiel, Daniel). In Leviticus and Numbers, it describes violations of religious or marital law, often involuntary, which require a guilt offering. In Chronicles and Ezekiel, it denounces the serious and conscious infidelity of Israel or its kings towards the Lord and His covenant. The word emphasizes the seriousness of sin: it is not a mere deviation, it is a personal betrayal towards God or towards someone to whom one has committed.
H4603.portee: This word invites the reader to understand sin not merely as a simple mistake, but as a rupture of relationship — a betrayal towards God with whom we have a covenant. It reminds us that God trusts us and that sin personally affects that trust. Recognizing one's infidelity is the first step towards forgiveness and the restoration of the covenant.

sens: Breach of trust towards a person, particularly in marriage
Violation of an obligation or covenant
Betrayal or treachery
Failure to be faithful to God
Transgression of divine law
Guilt resulting from a disloyal act
H4604.detail:
1. Marital infidelity: a woman who cheats on her husband breaks the bond of trust that unites them (Numbers 5:12, 5:27). It is an act that defiles and renders guilty.
2. A betrayal or treachery: when one violates a covenant or obligation towards someone, one commits infidelity. Achan is a typical example: he betrayed the trust of the people of Israel by taking the goods that God had consecrated (Joshua 22:20).
3. A transgression against God: it is failing in the faithfulness owed to the Lord, refusing to obey His word. Saul died for this infidelity: he did not keep God's commandments and consulted the dead instead of trusting Him (1 Chronicles 10:13).
4. A guilt that renders impure: infidelity defiles the one who commits it, whether directed against a man or against God. It calls for atonement, a guilt offering (Leviticus 5:15).
5. The sin that provokes God's judgment: when a nation or its people engage in infidelity, God may withdraw His blessing and send famine or destruction (Ezekiel 14:13).
H4604.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of "exceeding a limit," of "transgressing." Infidelity is therefore fundamentally a crossing of what was permitted, a violation of boundaries. It is an act of betrayal towards the one from whom trust has been received. The word is used for any breach of loyalty: towards a spouse, towards the people, but especially towards God who established His covenant with Israel.
H4604.emploi: This word appears 28 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical and prophetic books. It primarily denotes marital infidelity (Numbers 5), which defiles the woman and renders the couple impure. But it quickly expands to encompass any betrayal of a covenant: Achan who steals sacred goods (Joshua 7 and 22), Saul who disobeys God (1 Chronicles 10:13). The prophets, particularly Ezekiel, use it to describe Israel's infidelity towards its God: the people have violated the covenant and deserve judgment. Infidelity always calls for atonement or punishment, as it creates guilt before the one who has been betrayed.
H4604.portee: This word reminds us of the seriousness of failing in a covenant relationship. For the Christian, it evokes not only marital fidelity but especially fidelity towards God. Our relationship with God is based on His covenant: to betray Him is to render ourselves guilty and impure. That is why confession and atonement are essential. This word calls for vigilance: keeping the covenant means remaining attached to the one who has chosen us and who has loved us.

sens: The upper part of something, its top face
What is placed over, covering or concealing
Beyond a limit of size or age, from a certain point and upwards
The direction upwards, the space that rises
What comes after, the continuation or sequence
Above a person or thing, in a superior or dominant position
H4605.detail: 1. The upper part of something, its top face: it is simply the top of an object, what one sees when looking towards the summit. On Noah's ark, a "window" is placed at the "top" (Genesis 6:16), at the top of the structure. 2. What is placed over, covering or concealing: the word also denotes a covering that rests on something to protect it. The tent of meeting has a "covering of dolphin skins that is placed above" (Numbers 4:25), directly over the fabric. 3. Beyond a limit of size or age, from a certain point and upwards: it is used to count "from the age of twenty and above," all those who can serve (Numbers 1:24) — that is, twenty years and older. 4. The direction upwards, the space that rises: the word describes the movement or orientation towards the summit. The seraphim stand "above" the Lord in Isaiah's vision (Isaiah 6:2), in the space that overshadows Him. 5. What comes after, the continuation or sequence: by extension, the word can denote what follows chronologically. The Spirit of the Lord seized David "in the sequence" (1 Samuel 16:13), from that moment onward. 6. Above a person or thing, in a superior or dominant position: the word also expresses spatial or hierarchical superiority. The oxen carried the sea, "all the back part" being inside (2 Chronicles 4:4) — literally, the rear and upper part.
H4605.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to be on high" or "to ascend." In Hebrew, it is a very ancient and fundamental word: the same root appears in words related to height, to what rises or exceeds. The Hebrew word עַל ("al") — which means "on" — shares a similar idea: the position from above, superiority. This term expresses one of the simplest and most constant spatial images in the Bible: that of verticality, of high and low.
H4605.emploi: The word appears 134 times in the Hebrew Bible, with remarkable frequency in the books of law and history. It is frequently used in the censuses of the Book of Numbers, where it counts "from the age of twenty and above" for warriors (Numbers 1:24, 3:15, 4:3, etc.). It is also found in descriptions of the Tabernacle and the Temple (Exodus 25:20, 37:9; 1 Kings 7:3, 7:11), where the word indicates the position of covers, crowns, or upper parts. In historical and poetic passages, it describes the vertical direction — "the heaven above" (Deuteronomy 4:39, Isaiah 6:2) — or the chronological order. Its use in the Segond translations shows a beautiful flexibility: "high," "above," "on top," "sequence," depending on the precise context.
H4605.portee: This simple word reminds us that the Bible envisions the universe according to a vertical order: heaven above, earth below, God dominating all creation. When speaking of what is "above," one silently affirms a hierarchy and a dependence: what is below looks towards what is above. That is why "above" becomes an image of power, blessing, and providence. Understanding this spatial vocabulary helps the reader grasp how the Bible conceives the relationship between God and the world.

sens: The moment when the sun descends below the horizon at the end of the day
The decline of the day, the transition from light to darkness
H4606.detail:
1. The setting of the sun is the concrete moment when the star descends below the horizon at the end of the day. It is the image of movement downwards: the sun "goes down" and disappears. In Daniel 6:14, King Darius tries to save Daniel "until the setting of the sun," that is, until the end of the day.
2. By extension, the setting marks a transition: the passage from light to darkness, from activity to rest. It is the moment that closes a period, symbolically important: the king presses his efforts before night falls.
H4606.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "to go down, descend." This image of downward movement naturally applies to the sun that plunges below the horizon at the end of the day. The word can also denote other downward movements.
H4606.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 6:14, to denote the setting of the sun. It is a concrete and temporal term: it situates an action within the day, marking the limit between day and night. The context shows urgency: the king tries to save Daniel before time runs out and night arrives — the moment when the decrees of the Medes and Persians were to be enforced.
H4606.portee: This verse illustrates how night was once a limit, an impassable boundary for action. It underscores the dramatic tension of the narrative and, for the Christian reader, reminds us that God controls time: no human limit, no deadline can stop His plan of deliverance.

sens: To raise up
To lift hands in prayer or blessing
H4607.detail: 1. The word describes the action of raising something up, putting it in a high position. 2. In the text of Nehemiah 8:6, it specifically refers to lifting hands toward heaven: this is a gesture that accompanies prayer and expresses both praise, invocation, and surrender to God. Ezra blesses the Lord, and all the people lift their hands in response, before bowing down — the act of lifting precedes and prepares for humility.
H4607.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of lifting, elevating. In Hebrew, this gesture of raised hands is a very expressive body language: it signifies openness, calling, and offering oneself. This image is found in many contexts of prayer and communion with God.
H4607.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Nehemiah 8:6, during a great religious assembly after the return from exile. It is a solemn moment: the Law has just been read before all the people, Ezra blesses the Lord, and the collective reaction is immediate — the hands are raised together, then everyone bows down to the ground. The gesture expresses a complete adoration of the people, which goes through elevation and then lowering.
H4607.portee: This word reminds us that prayer is not just a matter of words: it is also a body language. Lifting hands to God is turning to Him with confidence, positioning one's body to listen and obey. This gesture, filled with respect and hope, invites the believer not to pray only in secret, but sometimes to manifest their faith through visible gestures.

sens: the action of going up, a path that leads upward
slope, incline, hill
stairs or steps to access a high place
a rising passage between two regions or two cities
H4608.detail:
1. The ascent is primarily the physical action of going up, progressing upward. It is the path taken to climb a slope: in Joshua 10:10, one ascends the road leading to Beth-Horon, a direction that implies an ascent.
2. The word also designates the slope itself, the terrain that rises: in 2 Chronicles 20:16, the hill of Ziz is an ascent by which the enemy must advance.
3. In buildings and fortifications, an ascent is a staircase or a series of steps: in Ezekiel 40:31, there are eight steps to ascend to the temple gate.
4. Finally, an ascent can be a strategic or geographical passage between two places, often named: in Joshua 18:17, the ascent of Adummim is a place that is crossed when going up, and in Nehemiah 12:37, it is by the ascent of the wall that one accesses the city of David.
H4608.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root עלה (alah), which means "to go up, to ascend." It is a natural image: the body that rises, the path that climbs, everything that ascends. The same root gives "ascent," "one who ascends," and the verb "to ascend" itself. It is a word deeply rooted in the physical experience of terrain and movement.
H4608.emploi: The word appears 18 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the historical and prophetic books. It often describes a geographical passage: a road that ascends (Joshua 10:10, 1 Samuel 9:11), a landmark path between two cities (Joshua 18:17, 2 Kings 9:27). It is also used for the stairs or steps of a building, such as in the temple (Ezekiel 40:31, 40:34, 40:37). Sometimes, it is synonymous with "hill" or "slope" (2 Chronicles 20:16). The meaning does not change much: it is always a movement or a path upward.
H4608.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, movement and physical effort are concrete realities of the journey. Ascents are obstacles, memorable passages, named places. For the believer, this invites us to see that ascending to God, directing oneself toward Him, requires effort, a heart orientation — an image that will later be found in the Psalms of ascent.

sens: What comes to mind, an idea that arises
The hidden intentions of the heart
The plans or projects one forms
H4609A.detail:
1. The word literally designates what "rises" — a thought that emerges in the mind, like something that comes to consciousness. In Ezekiel 11:5, God says to the prophet: "What comes to your mind, I know," meaning the ideas that come to your mind, even the most secret ones.
2. By extension, it describes the intimate intentions that one harbors in their heart and often hides from others. It is what truly occupies our mind, beyond what we say.
3. The word can also evoke the projects or plans that one forms — what "rises" within us as a design or will before it materializes into actions.
H4609A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to rise," "to elevate." The image is that of a thought rising from the heart to consciousness, like something that springs from our depths. It is a living thought, in motion, not a mere passive reflection. Ancient Hebrew thus saw the birth of ideas: they "rise" from within oneself.
H4609A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 11:5. The context is that of a prophetic word: God accuses the exiles of Judah of harboring rebellious thoughts and bad intentions. By saying "what comes to your mind," God affirms that He knows not only what people say but also what they secretly think. This passage emphasizes divine knowledge: nothing of our thoughts escapes God, even what is hidden deep within us.
H4609A.portee: This word reminds the reader that God sees our thoughts even before we express them. There is nothing secret before Him: He knows not only our actions and words but also the ideas that arise within us. It is both a call to honesty — since our thoughts betray us — and a source of comfort: God knows us completely, even in our most hidden intentions.

sens: step or stair that one ascends
marked divisions on a sundial
floors or levels of a building
progression from one point to another
spiritual ascent or rise
song sung during pilgrimages to the festivals in Jerusalem
H4609B.detail: 1. A step or stair: this is the most basic meaning of the word. In Exodus 20:26, God forbids the priest from ascending the altar by steps, so that his nakedness may not be uncovered while ascending the stairs; this shows the practical function of the word to designate the stages of an ascent. 2. The divisions of the sundial: the word refers to the visible graduations on the instrument. In 2 Kings 20:11, the shadow "goes back ten degrees" on the sundial of Ahaz, marking a miracle where time reverses. 3. The floors of a building: in the descriptions of Ezekiel's temple or the royal throne, the word counts the stacked levels (Ezekiel 40:22: "one ascended by seven degrees"). 4. The progression from one state to another: the word expresses a gradual passage, a succession of degrees or steps. 5. A symbolic ascent or rise: particularly in the psalms, it evokes the movement of the soul rising toward God. 6. A pilgrimage song: the "Songs of Ascents" (Psalms 120 to 134) are sung by pilgrims ascending to Jerusalem for the festivals; the title recalls both the physical movement upward and the spiritual journey toward the House of God.
H4609B.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to ascend" or "to rise." Its fundamental image is that of upward movement, progression toward higher ground. The degrees or steps are the material stages that embody this ascent. In the Greek Old Testament, it often corresponds to the Greek "anabathmós," which has the same root "ana" (upward) and "bathmos" (step). This family of words appears in many biblical contexts related to ascent and progression.
H4609B.emploi: The word appears 38 times in the Old Testament, first in architectural and material contexts: stairs of the altar (Exodus 20:26), steps of the royal throne (1 Kings 10:19-20, 2 Chronicles 9:18-19), degrees of the temple gate (Ezekiel 40 passim). It then takes on a figurative value in the Psalms, where the 15 "Songs of Ascents" (Psalms 120-134) transform the physical ascent to Jerusalem into an image of the spiritual ascent of the soul toward God. Amos 9:6 broadens the meaning by speaking of the "degrees" or levels of heaven itself. The word thus evolves from the concrete (step, stair) to the symbolic (spiritual progress, elevation of the soul).
H4609B.portee: For the Christian reading the Bible, the word "degree" reminds us that our path to God is not a leap, but a progressive ascent. The Songs of Ascents invite us to see each step of the spiritual life, each prayer and each act of obedience, as a step that brings us closer to the divine presence. It is an encouragement: holiness is not just a distant summit, it is a succession of accessible degrees, each elevating us higher.

sens: mountain pass in the south of Palestine
boundary between territories
H4610.detail:
1. Akrabbim refers to a pass or ascent in the desert region of southern Palestine, near Kadesh-Barnea. Its name literally means "ascent of scorpions," which likely evokes the dangers of this arid and rocky terrain. It is an important geographical landmark, mentioned in the description of the borders of the promised land (Numbers 34:4 and Joshua 15:3).
2. This passage serves as a territorial boundary: it marks the separation between lands assigned to different peoples. In Judges 1:36, it delineates the territory of the Amorites, showing that the region was a contested issue between Israel and neighboring peoples.
H4610.origine: The compound name literally means "ascent" (maaleh) and "scorpions" (akrabim). This designation likely evokes the hostile and dangerous nature of the terrain — scorpions are common in the desert areas of Palestine. The name retains its descriptive and geographical character: it is a place defined by its natural appearance and its perils.
H4610.emploi: Akrabbim appears three times in the Bible, always in the context of delineating the borders of the promised land. In Numbers 34, God lists the boundaries of the territory that Israel is to conquer: Akrabbim marks the southeast point. Joshua 15 reiterates this description by setting the borders of the tribe of Judah. In Judges 1, the text mentions this passage again to situate the extent of the Amorite territory in relation to Israeli expansion. It is a stable and strategic landmark for understanding biblical geography.
H4610.portee: This place name reminds us that the possession of the promised land was not automatic: it required traversing difficult passages, defended by other peoples. For the reader, Akrabbim symbolizes the obstacles and dangers inherent in obedience and spiritual conquest. The very name evokes that the path of faith involves trials, but it is this path that God assigns to His people.

sens: what a person does, their act, their gesture
a manner of conduct, a practice, especially a bad one
the entirety of a person's works, which testify to their character
what results from an action, its consequences or fruits
H4611.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the concrete act that a person performs — what they do with their hands or will. In Deuteronomy 28:20, God promises trouble "in all the enterprises you undertake," meaning the actions one undertakes.
2. It also signifies a practice, a way of life, often repeated and bad. When Jeremiah urges to "each turn from your evil way and the wickedness of your actions" (Jeremiah 25:5), he speaks of habitual behaviors that must be abandoned.
3. The word encompasses the entirety of a person's conduct — their works taken as a whole, which reveal who they truly are. Ezekiel 36:31 says: "You will remember your conduct that was bad, and your actions that were not good" — it is an entire life that is being examined.
4. Finally, actions produce fruits or consequences: Isaiah 3:10 asserts "he will enjoy the fruit of his works," showing that acts bear fruit, whether good or bad.
H4611.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to do," hence its primary sense: what one does, the act accomplished. The same root is found in other Hebrew words related to action and work. The word always expresses a visible, concrete action that can be observed and whose consequences can be measured — which is why the Bible often uses it to speak of acts in judgment.
H4611.emploi: The word appears 41 times in the Old Testament, especially in the prophetic books (Jeremiah in particular) and the Psalms. It constantly recurs in calls to repentance: God asks the people to "turn from their evil actions" (Jeremiah 4:4, 7:3). It also appears in affirmations that God "searches the heart" and "repays each according to the fruit of their works" (Jeremiah 17:10), showing that every act is known and judged. Actions can be good — those of the righteous (Isaiah 3:10) — or bad — those that distance from God. In the Psalms, we contemplate the "works" of God as His great acts in history (Psalms 77:12, 78:7).
H4611.portee: This word reminds the believer that every act counts. Nothing we do is hidden or insignificant: God sees, scrutinizes, and evaluates our actions. It is an invitation to moral vigilance and repentance — we cannot change the present or the future if we do not change our acts. But it is also a promise: the righteous who act well "will enjoy the fruit of their works," and this fruit comes from God Himself.

sens: Position or place one occupies in a hierarchy or organization
Role or office to which one is assigned, particularly in worship or temple service
Position from which one exercises responsibility
Charge or task that one regularly fulfills
H4612.detail: 1. The word designates the position or place one holds in an organization — it conveys the idea of 'holding a position'. In 1 Kings 10:5 and 2 Chronicles 9:4, it refers to the 'functions' or roles of the king's servants at his table. 2. It can mean the role or office to which one is assigned, especially in the context of worship. In 1 Chronicles 23:28, the Levites are 'placed' alongside the sons of Aaron to perform the 'service of the house of the Lord': this is their assigned function. 3. It is also the position from which one exercises responsibility or authority. In Isaiah 22:19, the Lord says to the one who occupies a position: 'I will thrust you from your office; the Lord will pull you down from your station' — it removes the one who holds this position. 4. The word can finally designate the charge or task that one regularly fulfills. In 2 Chronicles 35:15, the singers are 'in their place' and 'did not have to turn from their service': this is the role they continuously fulfill.
H4612.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of standing, taking a position, or establishing oneself in a place. It is related to words that describe a stance or a maintained position. The basic image is that of someone who 'stands' in a location — and from there, the notion of a post or function that one regularly occupies.
H4612.emploi: This word appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, primarily in royal narratives and passages related to the organization of worship. Three occurrences are found in the parallel accounts of the visit of the Queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10:5 and 2 Chronicles 9:4), where it describes the roles of the king's servants. Two others, in the books of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 23:28 and 2 Chronicles 35:15), use it to designate the posts assigned to the Levites in the service of the temple. One occurrence in Isaiah (22:19) uses it figuratively: to lose one's function. The context is always that of an assigned responsibility, a position held in an organized structure.
H4612.portee: This word reminds the reader that everyone has a place and a function assigned by God — whether in the family, the Church, or the community. It also emphasizes that this place is not permanent: it can be taken away (as in Isaiah 22:19) if one proves unworthy. It is an invitation to faithfully fulfill the role that is given to us.

sens: solid place to put one's foot
stable situation that allows one to resist or progress
ability to hold firm in adversity
H4613.detail:
1. The word literally designates a solid place where one can put their foot and find balance — like a stone or a firm surface. In Psalm 69:3, the psalmist sinks into the mud and seeks a point of support to avoid sinking: it is the image of a drowning person who can no longer find where to place their feet.
2. Figuratively, it is a stable situation, a solid base on which one can lean to resist or advance. One who has a point of support does not collapse under the weight of trials.
3. By extension, it means having the ability to hold firm, to maintain moral and spiritual balance when everything threatens to collapse.
H4613.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means 'to stand' or 'to take position'. It is the same verb that describes someone who remains firm, standing, who does not fall. The noun thus designates the place or state that allows for this stability — hence the idea of foundation, support, solid grip.
H4613.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalm 69:3. The psalmist, persecuted and desperate, compares himself to a man sinking into the mud: he has lost all point of support, all balance. The water overwhelms him, and he can no longer find where to hold on. It is a powerful image of complete anguish, the moment when even the ground abandons us.
H4613.portee: This word speaks to those going through moments when everything collapses: persecution, guilt, doubt, illness. The psalmist expresses that losing one's point of support means losing the ability to resist. But in writing this psalm, he addresses God: he calls upon the one who alone can give it — or restore it. For us, this word reminds us that our true stability does not come from our circumstances, but from God.

sens: heavy load that one carries or lifts
weight, physical heaviness
that which burdens, that which weighs on someone
H4614.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a concrete load, a burden that one carries or must lift. In Zechariah 12:3, Jerusalem is compared to a heavy stone that all the peoples attempt to lift — it is the image of a physical weight that cannot be borne without effort and pain.
2. By extension, the word evokes anything that is heavy, difficult to bear or handle. Spiritually, it represents what burdens, what weighs on the heart or shoulders of a person, like a moral burden or an overwhelming charge.
H4614.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that refers to the idea of carrying, bearing a weight. The nominal form emphasizes the weight itself, the mass that must be lifted. This type of word is common in Hebrew to speak of material burdens and, by metaphor, of the difficulties or sufferings one must endure.
H4614.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Zechariah 12:3. In this context of prophecy about Jerusalem, it paints the image of a city that has become so heavy, so formidable that all the peoples who attempt to conquer it leave their strength and are injured. It is a poetic way of saying that Jerusalem will be unshakeable and that those who attack it will fail.
H4614.portee: This word reminds us that certain realities — a city, a faith, a promise of God — can be so solidly established that they become insurmountable for those who oppose them. For the reader, it is an image of stability and divine power: God makes Jerusalem invincible, not by brute force, but by making it a weight that cannot be lifted without being crushed.

sens: Very deep hollow or cavity
Water abyss, marine depth
Figuratively: extreme distress, mortal danger
Unfathomable expanse
H4615.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a very deep hollow, a gaping cavity: in Psalm 69, the psalmist says, "I sink in the mire, where there is no standing; I have come into deep waters, and the flood overflows me" — the image is that of a pit filled with water where one sinks and cannot escape.
2. Applied to seas and oceans, it names the deep waters themselves, the abysses: Isaiah speaks of the "waters of the great abyss" that the Lord has dried up, and Ezekiel describes a city engulfed in the "depths of the waters."
3. Used figuratively, the word expresses the extreme depth of suffering or danger: Psalm 130 cries, "Out of the depths I have cried to You, O Lord!" — that is, from the state of the most serious, irreparable distress.
4. The word can also evoke the unfathomable immensity, that which escapes measurement — a space or reality so vast or obscure that it cannot be fathomed or traversed.
H4615.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be deep" or "to dig." The form here (in the plural with the suffix "ים") emphasizes the idea of multiplicity or intensity: the depths, the entirety of deep parts. The underlying image is that of digging, of that which sinks and escapes sight — hence the frequent association with danger, darkness, and inaccessibility.
H4615.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Psalms and the prophets. It has two main uses: literally, it names the deep waters (Isaiah 51:10 and Ezekiel 27:34, where it refers to the seas or their depths); metaphorically and in a context of prayer or lamentation, it expresses an extreme situation of distress, where the believer sees himself engulfed by misfortune (Psalms 69:3, 69:15, 130:1). In these cases, the abyss becomes an image of perdition from which only God can rescue the psalmist.
H4615.portee: This word teaches the Christian reader that distress can be expressed without shame before God: it is a reality, a formidable depth. But its use in the Psalms also shows that crying out from the abyss to God is to acknowledge His power to rescue the believer — it is a call for help that presupposes faith in divine deliverance.

sens: expresses purpose, intention: so that, with a view to
expresses reason, motive: because, due to
expresses stakes or interest: for the honor of, for the good of
H4616.detail: 1. The word indicates a sought objective or intention. The one who acts does so for this specific purpose. Thus Abraham says to Sarah: "Say you are my sister, in order that it may go well with me" (Genesis 12:13) — he wants to achieve this result. God makes Israel wander for forty years in the desert "in order to humble and test him" (Deuteronomy 8:2) — this is the divine purpose. 2. The word can also express the cause or reason why something happens or is stated. In the Psalms, the Lord "restores my soul" and leads me "for His name's sake" (Psalms 23:3) — it is His name that is the reason for His action. 3. Sometimes it emphasizes for what stakes or interest one acts: God calls Abraham "in order that he may command his children and his household" (Genesis 18:19) — this is the end for which God chooses him.
H4616.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of "sight" or "view" — the one who acts looks towards a goal, an end. It is used in construction with other words to mark the relationship between an action and its objective or cause. It is a fundamental grammatical tool for expressing the logical link between acts and their reasons or results.
H4616.emploi: This word is used 252 times in the Hebrew Bible, notably in the Torah (Moses) and in the historical books. It appears everywhere the Bible explains why something is ordered, done, or promised. With action verbs (say, do, command), it introduces the purpose: "Say you are my sister, in order that..." (Genesis 12:13). With speech verbs (say, speak), it explains the reason: "for His name's sake" (Psalms 23:3). With nouns or events, it specifies the stakes: "in order that you may remember His commandments" (Numbers 15:40). The meaning can vary slightly depending on the context, from the intended purpose to the cause or reason, but it always links two things by showing why one leads to the other.
H4616.portee: This word helps the reader understand God's intention or human motivation behind the reported acts. It reminds us that nothing in sacred history is gratuitous: every command, every trial has a purpose, often pedagogical or revelatory. This invites the believer to seek the meaning of the trials he goes through — they are not random, but directed towards transformation or deeper knowledge.

sens: Word spoken in response to a question or statement
Ability or action to respond
Intention or objective
H4617.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very concrete: it is the word addressed to someone who has just spoken, either to respond to a question or to react to a statement. In Proverbs 15:1, "A soft answer turns away wrath" shows that the quality of this answer — here its softness — can transform a tense situation. Job 32:5 describes the three friends who have "no more answer" to give, meaning they have no arguments left to oppose.
2. The word also designates the very ability to respond, the aptitude to find the appropriate words. In Job 32:3, Elihu's anger is kindled because his three friends "found nothing to answer" — they could not formulate a suitable reaction to Job's misfortunes.
3. Proverbs 16:4 uses the word in a broader sense: "The Lord has made everything for its purpose" — here, the answer becomes the intention, the objective for which something exists. It is the intended outcome, the design behind an action.
H4617.origine: The word comes from the root עִנָה ("to answer"), which evokes the idea of turning one's attention towards someone else, of facing them while speaking. The form מַעֲנֶה (ma'aneh) is the noun: it is what results from the act of answering, the answer itself. This root appears throughout the Hebrew Bible to describe the act of speaking in return or addressing someone, notably in the dialogues of the patriarchs with God.
H4617.emploi: The word appears 7 times, almost exclusively in the wisdom books: Job and Proverbs. In the debate between Job and his friends (Job 32:3, 32:5), it designates the argument, the word of defense that the three friends fail to provide in response to Job's protests — they remain without answer. In Proverbs, the word takes on a more moral and pedagogical nuance: the answer becomes a tool of wisdom, and its quality (soft or hard) determines its effect (Proverbs 15:1, 15:23). Proverbs 16:1 reminds us that while man prepares his plans, it is the Lord who gives the answer that the mouth speaks — the true word comes from God. Finally, in Proverbs 16:4, the word expands to the idea of cosmic design: everything the Lord creates, He created for a purpose (including the wicked).
H4617.portee: For the Christian reader, this word illuminates two important dimensions of life. First, the importance of the right word: a good answer, given at the right time and with the right tone, can change a situation from anger to peace — this is the art of wise communication, where the Christian learns to weigh his words. Secondly, the reminder that our words do not come solely from us: it is God who ultimately gives the true answer, the one that matters. This invites dependence on Him rather than trusting solely in our arguments.

sens: A groove dug in the ground by a plow
A deep trace or mark left on a surface
Figuratively, suffering or pain inflicted on someone
H4618.detail:
1. A furrow is the groove that a plow digs in the earth when cultivating a field. It is the work of the farmer preparing the soil for sowing. In 1 Samuel 14:14, it likely refers to a plowed surface where a battle takes place.
2. The word can more broadly refer to any deep mark or trace, like that left by an instrument on a surface. It is a visible and lasting incision.
3. Figuratively, furrows become the image of sufferings inflicted on someone: in Psalms 129:3, the psalmist says, "The plowers plowed upon my back; they made long furrows," evoking the blows received as traces engraved in the flesh, lasting marks of persecution.
H4618.origine: The Hebrew word מַעֲנָה (maanah) comes from a root that denotes the work of the land and plowing. It is related to other Hebrew terms concerning agriculture and land preparation. The image is that of the plowshare creating regular and deep furrows in the earth. This simple image of rural work naturally extends figuratively to describe any grave or lasting trace.
H4618.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in a context of trial or suffering endured. In 1 Samuel 14:14, it serves as a geographical or tactical marker in battle. But it is in Psalms 129:3 that it takes on its full figurative power: the psalmist uses it to describe the persecutions he has suffered, transforming the image of plowing into a symbol of oppression. The furrow thus becomes the lasting trace of pain, just as plowing leaves its mark in the earth. This rarity and concentration in contexts of suffering show that the word carries a strong emotional weight.
H4618.portee: This image of the furrow traced on the back of the persecuted speaks deeply to the heart of one who suffers: it acknowledges that the blows received leave traces, both visible and invisible. But by using an agricultural metaphor, the psalmist also reminds us that plowing prepares for the future harvest—an hope hidden beneath present suffering. For the believer, this reveals that God sees every trace of injustice done to His children and that pain, far from being lost, can bear fruit.

sens: son of Ram in the genealogy of Judah
H4619.detail: 1. Maats is a man from the tribe of Judah, living during the time of the divided monarchy. He is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:27, where he appears in the genealogical list of the descendants of Jerachmeel.
H4619.origine: The name Maats means "anger" in Hebrew. It belongs to the list of ancestors of Judah and represents one of the many generations that connect the patriarchs to the kings of Israel.
H4619.emploi: Maats appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:27. He is presented as the son of Ram (who is himself the son of Jerachmeel) and the brother of Jamin and Eker. His name appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, intended to show family ties and the continuity of God's people through the generations.

sens: Place or state of physical and moral suffering
Torment, deep anguish
H4620.detail:
1. The word designates a place or situation marked by suffering and sorrow. In Isaiah 50:11, the men who have turned away from God and have kindled their own fire (that is, who have followed their own plans) will ultimately lie down in pain—a state of misery and regret from which they cannot escape.
2. More broadly, this word evokes the torment and anguish that seize the one who suffers, particularly when that suffering comes from God's judgment. It is not only physical but affects the whole soul.
H4620.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root עצב (ʿatsav), which fundamentally means "to be in pain" or "to be afflicted." The form מַעֲצֵבָה (ma'atsvéva) is a feminine noun that designates the place or state where this affliction reigns. This root belongs to a family of Hebrew words speaking of the pain of the heart and sorrow.
H4620.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 50:11. It occurs in a context of divine judgment: the prophet Isaiah warns those who refuse to walk in the light of God and who build their own path. The "pain" upon which they will lie down is the inevitable consequence of their rebellion—not an arbitrary punishment, but the natural fruit of a life turned away from the Lord.
H4620.portee: This verse invites the believer to reflect on the consequences of their distance from God. It reminds us that seeking our own way rather than God's leads only to torment and desolation. It is a benevolent warning: returning to the light of God is the only remedy for this pain.

sens: Sharp metal tool fixed to a wooden handle, used for splitting wood
The action of cutting or chopping
H4621.detail:
1. The axe is the tool of the worker: a forged metal object fitted with a handle that allows for splitting, cutting, or shaping wood. In Isaiah 44:12, the blacksmith makes an axe by forging it with a hammer, then the worker uses it to work the wood in Jeremiah 10:3—this is the ordinary instrument of the carpenter or the lumberjack. The image is one of brute force, the tool that imposes its will on the material.
2. The meaning sometimes expands to the action of cutting or dividing itself, to the gesture of bringing down what must be cut. But in the Hebrew Bible, the word remains primarily concrete: it is first and foremost the axe as an object.
H4621.origine: The Hebrew word מַעֲצָד comes from a root that means to cut or chop. It belongs to the family of verbs of violent action: it is the name of the tool that accomplishes this work. The underlying image is that of a clean separation, a decisive division—the tool that divides.
H4621.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible: in Isaiah 44:12 and Jeremiah 10:3, both in contexts of woodwork. In Isaiah, it is the object made by the blacksmith; in Jeremiah, it is the tool of the worker shaping the wood. In both cases, the axe symbolizes ordinary human work and the transformation of creation by the hand of man. The usage remains very concrete and has nothing symbolic or eschatological about it.
H4621.portee: The axe reminds us that all manual work, even the simplest, requires knowledge, strength, and skill. These two verses show the Bible's respect for the artisan and the worker—the one who forges the axe with intelligence and the one who uses it with dexterity accomplish a worthy work. It is an invitation to see work, even when arduous, as participation in the order of creation.

sens: that which stops, blocks, or holds someone back
that which deprives of freedom of action
obstacle or hindrance to divine power
H4622.detail:
1. The word literally designates that which holds or stops: a barrier, a physical restraint. Jonathan uses it to say that nothing hinders the Lord from saving, meaning that no external limit can block His action (1 Samuel 14:6).
2. In a broader sense, it refers to anything that hinders, opposes, or limits someone in their plans or journey: a restraint, an impediment.
3. The word can also evoke a deprivation of freedom or movement: being held captive, with no possibility of advancing.
H4622.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to tighten," "to enclose," or "to reduce." It is formed as an action noun, like those that describe the effect of an action rather than its subject. The same root generates other words related to confinement, limitation, or detention. It is a rare word in the Bible, making its use in 1 Samuel 14:6 all the more significant.
H4622.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Samuel 14:6. Jonathan uses it to affirm that nothing hinders the Lord from saving His people, whether they have few or many warriors. Thus, it is a word that emphasizes the absence of limits or obstacles: the Lord knows no hindrance. This rare phrase makes the statement all the more striking — it expresses the absolute confidence that no human weakness can restrict divine power.
H4622.portee: This word reminds us that no external circumstance, no fleshly weakness, no small number can hinder God's will. When we feel blocked or limited, we can remember with Jonathan that God has no hindrance: He can save us and give us victory through means that seem the weakest to us.

sens: Dominion over one's own spirit, the ability to control one's impulses and desires
State of one who maintains control over their passions and reactions
H4623.detail:
1. Dominion over one's own spirit, the ability to control one's impulses and reactions — It is the faculty of restraining oneself, not being carried away by anger, covetousness, or momentary impulse. In Proverbs 25:28, the man who lacks this self-control is compared to a city without walls: he is vulnerable, exposed to all assaults.
2. State of one who maintains control over their passions and reactions — More broadly, it is the mastery one exercises over oneself, the ability to dominate one's heart and inner movements to act wisely rather than impulsively.
H4623.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to tighten," "to embrace," or "to restrain." This primary sense of "limitation" or "restriction" has expanded to the idea of self-control: one who possesses self-control firmly holds the reins of their own movements. The image evokes a brake, a firm grip on what might escape.
H4623.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 25:28. It is placed in a context of wisdom where the author lists the marks of true strength: he who masters his spirit is stronger than he who conquers a city. The rarity of the term shows that it is a quality of paramount importance, a pinnacle of virtue according to the sages of Israel.
H4623.portee: For the Christian, this verse reveals that true strength is not measured by domination over others, but by self-control. It is an invitation to guard one's heart, to cultivate inner discipline and restraint, especially in moments of provocation or temptation. This self-control is a mark of wisdom and spiritual maturity.

sens: A low barrier installed along an edge, a roof, or a bridge, to prevent people from falling.
By extension, a protection against danger or accident.
H4624.detail: 1. A railing is a low fence, typically made of stone, wood, or metal, placed at the edge of a roof, terrace, gallery, or bridge. It serves to keep people and objects from falling. In Deuteronomy 22:8, the Law of Israel commands the builder of a new house to place a railing around the roof: it is a concrete and necessary safety measure, as flat roofs were common living spaces. 2. Figuratively, the railing represents divine protection against evil or danger. It symbolizes the safeguards that God places in His Law to preserve His people from misfortune and guilt.
H4624.origine: The Hebrew word מַעֲקֶה (maaqeh) comes from a root meaning "to climb" or "to rise." The railing is thus literally that which "rises" along the edge, which elevates to protect. It is a concrete object of ordinary construction in ancient Israel, particularly important in a country where houses had flat roofs used as terraces for daily living.
H4624.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 22:8. It is found in the context of civil safety laws that Moses teaches the people before their entry into the Promised Land. The railing illustrates the biblical principle that the owner of a house must take care of those who visit and avoid shedding innocent blood. It is a practical law, not an abstract symbol: it shows that God's Law is concerned with the details of ordinary life and the protection of others.
H4624.portee: This command reveals that in God's eyes, the prevention of accidents and responsibility towards others are moral and important. It invites the believer to reflect on their responsibilities: how do they protect those who enter their home, both physically and spiritually? It is a call to prudence and love for one's neighbor in even the small things.

sens: Place or path that is not straight, winding or difficult
Difficulty, obstacle on the road
Image of trial or spiritual confusion
H4625.detail:
1. The word concretely designates a path that turns and curves, a rough terrain that is difficult to traverse — the opposite of a straight and level road. In Isaiah 42:16, God promises to transform the "crooked places" into level ground: it is about making passable what was winding and painful.

2. Figuratively, these crooked paths represent the obstacles and complications encountered by one who journeys. They embody all that makes the walk confusing, laborious, uncertain.

3. In the prophetic context, the crooked places finally evoke spiritual trial or the human condition marked by doubt and wandering — which God promises to straighten and clarify by His grace.
H4625.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be bent, to be inclined, to twist." It belongs to the same family as other Hebrew words that describe curvature, obliquity, or deviation. The image is very physical: something that is not in alignment, that deviates from the straight line.
H4625.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 42:16. It is found in a passage of consolation addressed to the exiles: God assures the blind and the lost that He will guide them on unknown paths and will transform darkness into light and crooked paths into level ground for them. This unique context shows how the divine promise straightens what was bent, clarifies what was confused, and makes possible what seemed impossible. The poetic and metaphorical use of the term makes it a powerful image of restoration.
H4625.portee: This word reminds the believer that crooked paths — trials, existential mazes, dark roads of life — are not the final word. God promises to straighten them, to illuminate them, and to guide even the blind. It is a word of comfort for those going through doubt or uncertainty: the Lord makes passable what seemed impassable, and transforms the obstacle into level ground.

sens: State of a person or thing that is bare, without clothing
Shameful exposure of the body, particularly during punishment or humiliation
Lack of protection, vulnerability
H4626.detail:
1. Nudity literally refers to the absence of clothing, the state of the body exposed and uncovered. This is the most direct physical meaning of the Hebrew word.
2. In the biblical context, nudity is often associated with shame and humiliation. When Nahum prophesies against Nineveh, he announces that the Lord will "uncover the skirts" of the city and show its "nakedness to the nations" (Nahum 3:5) — this is not merely a physical exposure, but a public stripping, a total humiliation before the peoples, a form of punishment and dishonor.
3. Figuratively, nudity evokes complete vulnerability, total lack of protection or defense — like a naked person facing their enemies.
H4626.origine: The Hebrew word מַעַר (ma'ar) comes from a root that expresses the idea of bareness and exposure. It is related to Hebrew terms that denote places or states devoid of covering. The basic image is that of a bare surface, without a veil — when applied to the body, it takes on the connotation of shameful exposure.
H4626.emploi: The word appears once in the Hebrew Bible, in the prophecy of Nahum against Nineveh (Nahum 3:5). It is used in a context of divine judgment: the prophet announces that the Lord will afflict the great city by revealing its nakedness to the nations, meaning delivering it to public humiliation and defeat. It is an act of judgment where nudity symbolizes the complete loss of power, dignity, and defense. The word thus carries a strong charge of shame and punishment.
H4626.portee: This word reminds us that nudity in the Bible is never neutral: it carries the idea of vulnerability, shame, and judgment. For the Christian, it illustrates how God's judgment on sin completely exposes, without mercy or veil — there is nothing that can hide before the Most High. It is a call to righteousness and the fear of God.

sens: Product intended for exchange or sale
Set of goods that are traded
The act of trading, commerce
H4627.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a material good, an object that is exchanged or sold. In Ezekiel 27:13, neighboring peoples bring slaves and bronze utensils in exchange for the merchandise of Tyre — these are the products that the city has to offer to foreign merchants.
2. Used in the plural, it evokes the totality of goods that a merchant possesses or that a trading city accumulates. Ezekiel 27:25 speaks of ships sailing for the "trade" of Tyre, meaning to transport and negotiate all its wealth and products.
3. The word can also refer to the activity itself, the exchange or trade: in Ezekiel 27:19, it speaks of what was "exchanged" with Tyre, and in 27:27 of "commerce" as an organized and flourishing activity.
H4627.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "to mix" or "to exchange." This root evokes the idea of bringing different things together, mixing them to form a market or transaction. That is why merchandise is what circulates, what changes hands, what creates commercial ties between peoples.
H4627.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in the prophet Ezekiel, notably in his long oracle against Tyre (Ezekiel 27). This concentration reveals the importance of the city of Tyre as an international trading center: all its verses deal with the flourishing trade of this port city. The word designates sometimes the goods exchanged (Ezekiel 27:13, 27:17), sometimes the commercial activity itself (Ezekiel 27:25, 27:27), showing that trade and merchandise are inseparable in ancient economy.
H4627.portee: This word reminds us that trade and material wealth hold an important place in the biblical world, but also that this earthly prosperity remains fragile and subject to God's judgment. Ezekiel's oracle against Tyre shows how a city built on the accumulation of merchandise and commercial wealth can fall. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation not to place trust in exchangeable material goods, but in what remains eternal.

sens: direction where the sun sets
region or territory located to the west
western limit of a place or building
H4628.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the cardinal point where the sun disappears on the horizon, the literal sense of "the west" (Psalms 103:12: "As far as the east is from the west"). It is the direction opposite to the rising sun, the natural landmark used by ancient peoples for orientation.
2. It applies to any region or territory located toward the west: lands, cities, regions that extend in that direction (1 Chronicles 7:28: the cities of Gezer and Shechem to the west of Bethel).
3. It also designates the western side or limit of a construction, fortification, or specific gate, as a precise architectural dimension (1 Chronicles 26:16: "The western side was assigned to Shuppim and Hosa," speaking of the gates of the Temple).
H4628.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of setting, of the fall of day. The Hebrew associates it with the image of the sun that lowers and disappears. This root is found in other words describing movements or positions downward. The word has settled into usage to designate the constant direction of the setting sun, and then everything located in that direction.
H4628.emploi: The word appears fourteen times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of Chronicles and Psalms, and sometimes in Isaiah and Daniel. It serves to specify geographical locations (cities to the west, western borders) and to situate the structures of the Temple or royal fortifications. In the Psalms, it uses this word poetically to evoke the infinite distance between the east and the west, symbolizing the removal of sins (Psalms 103:12). Isaiah uses the west as the extreme point from which God gathers His people, alongside the east (Isaiah 43:5).
H4628.portee: This word reminds us that God controls all creation, from east to west, and that no direction, no earthly limit escapes His gaze. For the Christian, the image of the east and west separated by an immense distance speaks of God's forgiveness: He removes our sins as far as the two horizons are from each other.

sens: open plain, uncovered terrain without obstacles
H4629G.detail: 1. The word refers to an open area of land, a plain without trees or buildings — the space that can be seen and traversed freely. In Judges 20:33, during a battle between Israelites, the men of Gibeah come out of the city to this open space to fight, allowing them to deploy in formation and see the enemy approaching.
H4629G.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of bareness or exposure — something that is laid bare, cleared, without covering. The same root gives rise to other words related to nakedness and lack of protection.
H4629G.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 20:33. It describes the military terrain where the battle takes place, a place where warriors have room to fight in open line, without being hindered by buildings or forest. The context suggests that this open space is a tactical advantage for deploying the troops.
H4629G.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of terrain in human strategies: even in biblical times, warriors chose their ground for battle. It invites us to reflect on how God governs history, including the material details that seem insignificant.

sens: flat and clear surface
empty area available for decoration or a motif
H4629H.detail:
1. The word designates an empty space, a surface without obstacles — in this case, on a piece of furniture or an object. In 1 Kings 7:36, it refers to the free spaces on the plates and panels of a bronze basin: these are the areas that the craftsman can engrave or decorate, between the edges or structural elements.
2. By extension, it refers to any bare, clear, and available surface that can be used or filled. The context shows that motifs (cherubim, lions, palms) are precisely engraved in these "spaces" to beautify the object.
H4629H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of exposure or nakedness — something exposed, without covering. It is a rare word in biblical Hebrew, painting the image of an open and available surface.
H4629H.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 7:36. It designates the free surfaces of the bronze basin that King Solomon had made for the Temple. The architectural context shows that these "spaces" are the areas that the craftsman intentionally leaves empty to adorn with figurative engravings — a practical and concrete notion related to the work of decoration.
H4629H.portee: This word reminds us that in the order of the Temple and the house of God, every detail matters, even the empty spaces intended to welcome the beauty of sacred art. It invites us to see the greatness of God reflected in the excellence of well-done work.

sens: Natural hollow in a mountain or rock, serving as shelter
Underground burial place, either dug or natural
Refuge for fugitives or fighters
