Den or lair of animals
H4631.detail:
1. A cave is primarily a natural hollow, a grotto carved into the mountain or rock. Lot takes refuge there with his daughters after the destruction of Sodom (Genesis 19:30), and David flees there from Saul to escape death (1 Samuel 24:4). It is a dark, secluded place where one hides or seeks shelter.
2. The cave also serves as a tomb: Abraham buries his father there, and it becomes the family burial site of Isaac and Jacob (Genesis 25:9; 49:29-32). It is called the "cave of Machpelah." It is a hollow carved into the rock, thus naturally protected, where the dead rest.
3. During wars and persecutions, the cave becomes a refuge. The men of Israel hide there to escape the Philistines (1 Samuel 13:6), and the five kings of Canaan take refuge there before being crushed by Joshua (Joshua 10:17). It is a secret place where one protects oneself from danger.
4. Rarely, the cave can be the den of a fierce beast: it can be referred to as a "lair" (Ezekiel 33:27). This is the most distant image, but it emphasizes that the cave is a natural refuge, whether for humans or animals.
H4631.origine: The Hebrew word מְעָרָה comes from a root that evokes digging, excavating (עור). It is a feminine noun. The word belongs to the vocabulary of daily life in Canaan, where caves are numerous and often inhabited. It is found in famous place names like "the cave of Machpelah" or "the cave of Adullam." Ancient vocabulary recognizes the cave as an element of the geographical landscape as natural as the mountain or valley.
H4631.emploi: The word appears 36 times in the Masoretic Hebrew text, mainly in the historical narratives of Genesis, Joshua, and Samuel. In Genesis, caves are linked to the patriarchs: Abraham buys the cave of Machpelah as a family burial site (Genesis 23-25), and it remains the tomb of the ancestors. In the historical books (Joshua, Samuel, Kings), the cave is the refuge of warriors or fugitives: Joshua traps the five kings there (Joshua 10), David hides there from Saul (1 Samuel 24), and Elijah retreats there at Mount Horeb (1 Kings 19:9). In times of crisis, it becomes the shelter of the people (1 Samuel 13:6 during the Philistine invasion, Judges 6:2 under Midian). The term thus always retains the same concrete meaning: it is a natural hollow, either for dwelling, hiding, or burying the dead.
H4631.portee: The cave in the Bible symbolizes both human fragility (one hides there to survive) and trust in God (David prays there without fear: Psalms 57:1; 142:1). It speaks to us of places where one withdraws to meet God in solitude or distress. It also reminds us of the importance that ancestors placed on burial: it is a concern of the patriarchs to rest, like Lot or Abraham, in the cave of the land that God promised them.

sens: locality or cave near Sidon in Phoenicia
H4632.detail: Meara is a region or geographical formation (possibly a cave or depression) located in the territory of the Sidonians, east of Sidon. It appears in the description of the lands that had not yet been conquered at the time when Joshua distributes the territories to the tribes of Israel (Joshua 13:4).
H4632.origine: The Hebrew name מְעָרָה (me'arah) literally means "cave" or "grotto": it comes from the root עָרָה (arah). The word designates either a real cave or perhaps a valley or rock formation characterized by cavities, near the Phoenician coast.
H4632.emploi: Meara appears only once in the Bible, in the list of territories that the Canaanites and Phoenicians still occupied at the time of Joshua. It is mentioned as a geographical landmark to establish the boundaries of the unclaimed land, between Sidon and Aphek. Its precise identification remains uncertain.

sens: Plan or project developed by the mind
Intention or design formed in the heart
H4633.detail:
1. The word designates a project or plan that one elaborates in one's mind — something conceived and organized mentally before being realized. In Proverbs 16:1, it refers to the plans formed in the heart of man: these thoughts, these intentions that one ruminates and prepares within oneself before putting them into action or expressing them in words.
2. The word emphasizes the personal and voluntary nature of the project: it is what one decides, what one arranges within oneself. The verse from Proverbs shows that even if man can form his plans, it is God who has the final word, particularly regarding the response one gives — what truly comes out of the mouth.
H4633.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of arranging, organizing, putting in order. This is why "project" captures this notion well: it is something that one arranges, that one orders in one's mind, a thoughtful plan rather than a mere passing thought. The same root can evoke preparation, material organization.
H4633.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 16:1. It specifically designates the projects or plans that a man conceives in his heart. The wisdom context of the book of Proverbs highlights the contrast between what man can plan and organize and what ultimately depends on God: man disposes (he forms his plans), but God ordains (he controls the outcomes, especially what one says).
H4633.portee: This word reminds believers of a fundamental truth: although we have the right and responsibility to think, to plan our actions, none of our projects escapes God's sovereignty. It does not invite inaction but trust: our plans matter, but it is God who ultimately disposes of them.

sens: Line of soldiers arranged in battle order
Group of fighters organized for war
Formation of troops ready for combat
Order and arrangement (in a context of ritual or material preparation)
H4634.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is that of a line or rank of soldiers. When two armies meet, they form in battle with their warriors aligned face to face: this is expressed in "Israel and the Philistines formed in battle, army against army" (1 Samuel 17:21).
2. By extension, the word designates the organized group of fighters themselves: the army of Israel facing that of the Philistines (1 Samuel 17:10). It refers to the entire troop, constituted and ordered for war.
3. The word can also simply evoke the field or place where the combat takes place: "on the battlefield" (1 Samuel 4:2) and "out of the ranks of the Philistines" (1 Samuel 17:23), where it refers to the space where the armies deploy.
4. In a more general register, the word describes any ordered arrangement or preparation: thus the lamps of the lampstand "prepared" (Exodus 39:37) are placed and arranged according to the prescribed order.
H4634.origine: The Hebrew word ma.a.rah comes from a root that expresses the idea of aligning, arranging in rows. It is close to ma.arah (מַעֲרָה, "army"), which shares the same family of meanings. The starting image is that of an orderly arrangement in lines, as when arranging objects or people according to a regular plan. This root is very active in the Old Testament to express military order.
H4634.emploi: This word appears seventeen times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of Samuel and in the context of the war between Israel and the Philistines. It is frequently used around the account of David and Goliath (1 Samuel 17), where it repeatedly describes the deployment and formation of the two enemy armies. Some uses refer to the battlefield itself (1 Samuel 4:2, 4:16), others to the entire group of fighters or their order (1 Samuel 17:10, 17:21, 17:23). One use is outside the war context: Exodus 39:37, where the word describes the ordered preparation of the lamps of the golden lampstand. This shows that the fundamental meaning of the word is that of an arrangement or a regulated disposition, whether military or ritual.
H4634.portee: This word reminds every reader that war is primarily a matter of order and organization: it requires coordinated, arranged men, in ranks. In the account of David and Goliath, the emphasis on the "armies" facing each other highlights the seemingly insurmountable inequality — until David, without armor or metal sword, steps forward alone against Goliath. Human arrangement and order are not everything: faith in God takes precedence over organized strength.

sens: arrangement, disposition in rows
set of breads placed on the table of the sanctuary
ritual offering of breads presented to God
H4635.detail:
1. The Hebrew word primarily denotes an arrangement or regular disposition in lines, as when placing objects side by side (Leviticus 24:6 speaks of "piles," meaning rows of bread).
2. In Israelite worship, it specifically refers to the twelve breads placed on the golden table of the sanctuary, arranged in two stacks of six, which the priest renewed every Sabbath (1 Chronicles 9:32 mentions the preparation of these breads).
3. These breads constitute a permanent offering, a sign of God's presence and the covenant with Israel; they are burned with incense as a memorial before the Lord (Leviticus 24:7 specifies that pure incense accompanies each stack).
H4635.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to arrange," "to put in order," or "to line up." The image is that of a regular and symmetrical arrangement. The term "showbread" (literally "breads of the row" or "exposed breads") emphasizes that these breads are constantly presented, placed before God on the table of the sanctuary as a sign of dependence and communion with Him.
H4635.emploi: This word appears nine times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in the historical books and the laws of worship (Leviticus and Chronicles). It always refers to the twelve ritual breads of the tabernacle or temple. In Leviticus 24:6-7, we see the details of their preparation and arrangement. In 1 Chronicles 9:32, the Levites are responsible for preparing them every Sabbath. In 2 Chronicles 2:4 and 29:18, the renewal of the showbread is part of the regular service of the restored temple. This worship was a perpetual ordinance for Israel, renewed every week.
H4635.portee: The showbread reminds the believer that God would remain at the heart of the people and that Israel was called to serve Him through a continual offering. These breads represent total dependence on God for daily bread and the people's commitment to live in His presence. This worship practice illustrates how serving God must be regular, orderly, and a constant priority in the life of the chosen people.

sens: The state of being without clothing, devoid of body covering
Figuratively, the condition of vulnerability and extreme destitution
H4636.detail:
1. The word literally denotes the absence of clothing, the uncovered body. In 2 Chronicles 28:15, war captives, stripped of everything during pillaging, are found "naked" — that is, without clothes or protection, in a state of total misery. The context shows that this nakedness is not ordinary nakedness: it is that of people reduced to slavery and indigence.
2. Beyond the physical sense, nakedness expresses in the Bible a deep vulnerability: that of one who possesses nothing and finds themselves exposed to shame, need, and scrutiny. It embodies absolute destitution — not only of the body but of dignity and security. It is not a neutral state, but a situation of distress.
H4636.origine: The Hebrew word ma'arom comes from a root that evokes the idea of being stripped or naked. In biblical Hebrew, nakedness is often associated with shame, vulnerability, or dispossession — never presented as an innocent or natural state. This term belongs to the semantic field of poverty and need.
H4636.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Chronicles 28:15. It refers to the war captives whom benevolent leaders from Samaria welcomed and clothed. The context is crucial: these men are naked because they were stripped during a military defeat. The compassion of the leaders towards these wretched individuals is manifested in restoring their clothing, food, and dignity. This unique passage illustrates how nakedness embodies the peak of destitution and vulnerability.
H4636.portee: This account teaches that recognizing the needs of others must lead to concrete action. Clothing, food, and care given to the naked remind us that following God involves seeing distress and responding to it. Jesus will take up this image in Matthew 25, where clothing the naked becomes an act of service to Christ Himself.

sens: Brutal shock, violent rupture
Sudden and spectacular destruction
H4637.detail:
1. The word denotes a brutal shock that breaks and destroys: in Isaiah 10:33, it is the violence with which the Lord breaks the branches of the "most elevated" trees — an image of overwhelming and unresisting power.
2. More broadly, it refers to the sudden and spectacular destruction of a power that seemed invincible, such as that of kings and empires: the word carries the idea of a collapse that is as rapid as it is brutal.
H4637.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the sharp and violent sound of a rupture, a fracture. It is rare in the Bible and seems to express a very concrete idea: that of an event that does not gradually cause harm, but strikes suddenly. The word belongs to the family of words that describe acts of force and oppression.
H4637.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 10:33. The prophet uses it to describe God's action of "breaking the branches violently" of the trees of the high mountains and hills. It is an act of the Lord that crushes the symbols of power and pride. The image is deliberately linked to the destruction of the kings of Assyria mentioned in the context of Isaiah.
H4637.portee: This word reminds us that human power, even the most imposing, cannot stand against the power of God. The Lord does not destroy slowly or gradually: when He acts, it is with a force that admits no resistance. For the believer, it is both a warning against pride and an assurance that God protects His people against the powers that oppress them.

sens: City of Judah
H4638.detail: Maarath is a small town in the mountainous region of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible (Joshua 15:59) among the cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the territory. Its name means "nakedness" or "bare place," perhaps evoking rocky terrain or a denuded area of the Judean heights.
H4638.origine: The name Maarath comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be naked" or "devoid." This etymology reflects the arid or clear landscape of the region where this locality was situated in the mountains of Judah.
H4638.emploi: Maarath appears only once in the Scriptures, in Joshua 15:59, in the context of the land distribution among the tribes of Israel after the conquest. It is listed among the six cities in the mountainous region of Judah assigned to the tribe of Judah, alongside Beth-Anoth and Elthekon. This brief mention would make it a locality of little importance, with no particular biblical narrative attached to it.

sens: Action of doing, concrete work accomplished by one's hands
Production, object made by this work
Business, trade, function regularly exercised
Moral action: what one does, good or bad
Powerful act, remarkable or miraculous achievement
Manifestation of divine power
H4639G.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the physical action of working, the daily effort: Noah will be called thus because he "will comfort us concerning our labor and the toil of our hands" (Genesis 5:29). It is the concrete labor, what one does with one's strength.

2. It also signifies the visible result of this work: the shaped object. In the Tabernacle, "they made for the entrance of the tent a curtain […] it was a work of embroidery" (Exodus 36:37). The word here refers to the tent, the covering, the priestly garment – everything that has been made.

3. It can describe a trade or function that one fulfills: when Pharaoh asks Joseph, "What is your occupation?" the Hebrew word used is this one (Genesis 47:3). It is the usual activity by which one earns a living.

4. It also characterizes the moral acts of a person: "Render to them according to their works and according to the wickedness of their deeds" (Psalms 28:4). The works reveal the heart: they can be just or evil.

5. It denotes powerful acts, exploits: "Let each generation celebrate your works, and declare your mighty acts!" (Psalms 145:4). These are the great deeds that mark history.

6. Finally, it specifically names divine action, creation, and God's intervention acts: "the work of my hands" (Isaiah 29:23), that is what God creates and accomplishes with His power.
H4639G.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to do" or "to act." It is very ancient and very common throughout the Old Testament. Its basic image is that of the hand at work: the work is what the hand brings forth. The Hebrew word enters into several compounds and always retains this central notion of action, production, concrete realization.
H4639G.emploi: This word is among the most frequent in the Old Testament (175 occurrences). It is first found prominently in the technical descriptions of the Tabernacle and its ornaments (Exodus 26-39): garments, embroideries, pieces of gold or bronze shaped. It is used for the daily work of humans and servants (Exodus 5:4-5, tasks of Pharaoh; 1 Samuel 25:2, occupation of a shepherd). It is very common in the Psalms and wisdom literature to speak of the acts of men (good or bad) and especially of divine works: what God creates, what He accomplishes for His people. The meaning varies little: it is always what one does or what one produces, whether human or divine.
H4639G.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to see that our actions matter: they reveal who we are and they will be judged. But above all, it turns the eyes toward the works of God – His creation, His deliverances, His miracles – to lead us to worship His power and wisdom. Contemplating the works of God is to recognize Him and fear His name.

sens: Act done, concrete gesture of a person
Work, labor, sustained effort
Enterprise, project or business
Result created, thing done or produced
Moral action or behavior subject to judgment
Acts of divine power, interventions of God
H4639K.detail:
1. The act, the concrete gesture: what a person does at a given moment. Abraham committed "acts that should not be committed" against Abimelech (Genesis 20:9) — specific and reprehensible gestures. It is the visible and defined action.
2. Work, sustained effort: the activity of one who labors and produces. It is the effort given to a task, the work of a day or a lifetime.
3. The business, the enterprise, the project: a situation or undertaking that occupies and engages. David says to Jonathan: "you will remain near the stone of Ezel" on the day of this "business" (1 Samuel 20:19), that is, of what is being plotted.
4. The product, the thing done: what exists because it has been done. Every created object, every visible result is a work.
5. The moral action, the judgment-worthy act: behavior considered from the perspective of good or evil. Ecclesiastes reminds us that "God will bring every work into judgment, concerning everything that is hidden, whether good or evil" (Ecclesiastes 12:16). It is the action that reveals the heart.
6. The act of divine power: the interventions, signs, and judgments of God. The psalmist cries: "I shall live and recount the works of the Lord" (Psalms 118:17), His merciful and saving acts.
H4639K.origine: The Hebrew word מַעֲשֶׂה (ma'aseh) comes from the root עשׂה (asah), which means "to do," "to act," "to accomplish." This root is very common in biblical Hebrew: it expresses the action of producing, realizing, creating. The word appears mainly in narratives where the acts of men or God structure history. The nominal form ma'aseh personifies the action: it is what exists because it has been accomplished.
H4639K.emploi: This word appears 47 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives (Genesis, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles), in poetry (Psalms, Proverbs), and wisdom literature (Job, Ecclesiastes). Its meaning varies according to the context. In historical narratives (Genesis 20:9, 1 Samuel 20:19), it designates specific acts, sometimes reprehensible. In the Psalms, it primarily evokes the "works" of God, His saving interventions (Psalms 118:17, 145:13). Ecclesiastes uses it to speak of human actions judged and evaluated in their vanity (Ecclesiastes 12:16). In the prophets, it can designate both the evil human actions (Isaiah 57:12) and the creative work of God (Isaiah 26:12). The word thus encompasses the punctual act, the sustained work, and the complex enterprise.
H4639K.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that every act counts: it is seen by God and will be judged. At the same time, it invites us to contemplate and celebrate the "works" of God, His acts of deliverance and justice, a source of assurance and praise. This calls us to act with conscience, knowing that our actions reflect our heart and that it is God who accomplishes the ultimate work of redemption.

sens: Priest of the tribe of Levi returning from exile
Son of Adiel and father of priestly descendants
H4640.detail: Maesaï is a priest from the tribe of Levi who lived at the time of the return from exile. His name means "work of the Lord" in Hebrew, reflecting the consecration of priests to divine service. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:12, where he is presented as the son of Adiel and the father of a priestly lineage that established itself in Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity. This priest is among those who participated in the restoration of worship at the temple.
H4640.origine: The Hebrew name Maesaï (מַעֲשַׂי) literally means "work of the Lord" (from ma'aséh, "work, labor"). It is a theophoric name — a name bearing the name of God — which expresses the belief that this child was a work accomplished by the Lord. In post-exilic priestly lists, theophoric names remained a common practice to remind the people of their dependence on God.
H4640.emploi: Maesaï appears only once in the scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 9:12. He is cited in a genealogical list of priests and Levites who settled in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile (circa 538 B.C.). This list enumerates the priestly families charged with the service of the restored temple. Maesaï thus represents one of these Levitical families that contributed to the revival of Israelite worship after the destruction of the first temple.

sens: Levitical musician during the time of King David
Man who bore this name in the history of Israel
H4641G.detail:
1. Maaséja is a Levite (member of the tribe dedicated to temple service) who lived during the time of King David. He was part of the musicians who played instruments during important religious ceremonies, notably during the transport of the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:18-20).

2. This name designates several other important men in the life of Israel over the centuries: priests, Levites, royal officers, and even descendants who signed the covenant with Nehemiah after the Babylonian exile. It is a name borne by servants of God at different times.
H4641G.origine: The name Maaséja literally means "work of the Lord" or "what the Lord has done." It is composed of two parts: "maasé" (work, action, labor) and "Yah" (short form of the name of God, the Lord). This type of theophoric name, that is, containing the divine name, was common in Israel and expressed the belief that the child was a work and a blessing from God.
H4641G.emploi: In the Bible, the name Maaséja appears about twenty times and designates many different people. The two passages in 1 Chronicles 15 mention him as a Levite musician who played stringed instruments (lyres) in religious service during the time of David. The same name is borne by other important figures: priests during the time of Ezra who had to correct their marriages with foreign women, royal officers under various kings of Judah, and high-ranking Levites. This multiplicity of bearers of the name Maaséja shows the importance of this family in the religious and political history of Israel, from the time of David until after the Babylonian exile.

sens: Character from the time of the divided monarchy, father of several important descendants

Several bearers of this name were priests and Levites, while others were military or civil leaders, reflecting the importance of this family in the Judean community.

sens: officer of King Uzziah responsible for counting the troops

H4641I.origine: The name Maaséja literally means "work of Jehovah" (from the Hebrew "maasé," work, labor, and the divine "Yah"). Although the same name is borne by at least twenty different individuals in the Old Testament (notably several priests during the time of Ezra, a Levite during the time of David, fathers of prophets, and other dignitaries), this Maaséja is distinguished by his unique appearance and specific military role. He represents those invisible yet indispensable high officials who enabled the king to govern and maintain his army.

sens: Son of King Ahaz of Judah, killed during the invasion of the kingdom by King Pekah of Israel

H4641J.emploi: Maaséja is the son of King Ahaz of Judah and the brother of Hezekiah. He appears only in 2 Chronicles 28:7, in the account of the invasion of Judah by Pekah, king of Israel, and Syria. H4641J.portee: The death of Maaséja reveals how the king's disobedience to God's commandments leads to tragic consequences not only for himself but also for his family and his people. sens: Man from the Exile and Return period
Priest or Levite who had married a foreign woman
H4641L.detail:

It also shows that the holiness demanded by God spares no one, not even the priests. For the Christian reader, it is a lesson on the importance of moral and spiritual purity, and on the grace of God that allows those who recognize their errors to return to Him.

sens: A man from the Exile and Return period, mentioned in Ezra 10:21
Priest from the family of Harim who had married a foreign woman

sens: Man who lived during the Exile and the Return

sens: Levite who taught the law to the people during the time of Nehemiah

It expresses the belief that this child is the work of God, His creation and gift. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, placing the person under the protection and action of God. Several generations of Maaséja attest to the persistence and transmission of this religious trust beyond the Exile.
H4641W.emploi: Maaséja is attested only once with this exact spelling in Nehemiah 12:42, during the ceremony of consecration of the rebuilt walls under the leadership of Nehemiah and Ezra. The text places him among the singers and musicians, suggesting his role in the restored worship. However, the name Maaséja (in various forms) belongs to a common family in the genealogies of the Exile and the return, and several people bear this name in the 6th-5th centuries B.C., holding priestly, Levitical, or administrative positions in the Judean community.
H4641W.portee: The name Maaséja reminds the reader that the Exile and the return are not a void or a break, but a time when God continues to act and transform His people. These Maaséja who restore the worship and government of Judah embody the faith that the Lord is always at work, that He works even in crises, and that hearts trusting in Him perpetuate His name and His work from generation to generation.

sens: Father of the priest Zephaniah during the reign of King Zedekiah of Judah
H4641X.detail: Maaséja is a man who lived during the time of the monarchy of Judah, during the reign of King Zedekiah. He is known as the father of Zephaniah, a high-ranking priest. Zephaniah appears several times in the events at the end of the kingdom of Judah: King Zedekiah sends him with other delegates to the prophet Jeremiah to ask him to intercede with God (Jeremiah 21:1 and 37:3). Zephaniah also receives a letter from Jeremiah addressed to the priests, of which Maaséja might have knowledge (Jeremiah 29:25).
H4641X.origine: The name Maaséja means 'work of the Lord' or 'the Lord has done'. It is formed from maa'aseh (work, act, deed) and Yah (abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah). This theophoric name expresses the father's faith in God's action. Several men bore this name in the Old Testament, notably priests and Levites during the time of Ezra and Nehemiah.
H4641X.emploi: Maaséja appears three times in the provided contexts, always referred to as the father of the priest Zephaniah. He lived under the reign of King Zedekiah, at the end of the kingdom of Judah (the last years before the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.). The context of the three mentions shows that his son Zephaniah plays an official role: the king chooses him as a messenger to the prophet Jeremiah, indicating that Zephaniah holds a position of authority among the priests. Although Maaséja is mentioned only as the father, his paternity situates his son in a noteworthy priestly lineage.

sens: Man living during the time of the Divided Monarchy, father of the false prophet Zedekiah
H4641Y.detail: Maaséja is a name borne by several characters in the history of Israel. In this specific passage, it designates the father of Zedekiah, a false prophet during the time of Jeremiah. In Jeremiah 29:21, the prophet Jeremiah receives the word of the Lord concerning Ahab and Zedekiah — the latter being the son of Maaséja — who deceive the people by prophesying lies in the name of God. Jeremiah announces that the Lord will deliver them to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, who will have them killed. This usage shows Maaséja as the father of a man who has turned away from true service to God.
H4641Y.origine: The name Maaséja means 'work of the Lord' or 'what the Lord has done'. It is composed of two Hebrew roots: 'ma'aséh' (work, action) and the abbreviated divine name 'Yah' (Lord). This is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God, which was common in Hebrew names. This type of name expressed the belief that the child was a blessing or act of God.
H4641Y.emploi: Maaséja is a very common name in post-exilic biblical texts, notably in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, where several characters bear this name — descendants of Jeshua, priests, Levites, officiants during the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem. However, the usage provided by the Segond 1910 specifically designates the father of the false prophet Zedekiah during the time of Jeremiah, in Jeremiah 29:21. This context is that of the exile to Babylon, where Jeremiah writes to the exiles to denounce the false prophets who deceive them. This Maaséja is mentioned only once in this role as a father, and serves to clearly identify which Zedekiah is in question — the false prophet, and not other namesakes.

sens: Son of Shallum, gatekeeper at the temple under the kings of Judah
H4641Z.detail: Maaséja is an officer of the temple in Jerusalem, responsible for the gatekeeping. In the account of Jeremiah, the prophet mentions him to locate a chamber of the temple: it is near the chamber of Maaséja, son of Shallum, that the chamber where the sons of Rechab slept was located, a family faithful to the commandments of their ancestor (Jeremiah 35:4). His role as a guardian shows the importance of watch positions at the temple, and his appearance in this context attests to his recognized position among the leaders of the sanctuary.
H4641Z.origine: The Hebrew name מַעֲשֵׂיָהוּ (Maaséja) literally means 'Work of the Lord' or 'What the Lord has done'. It is composed of עָשָׂה (to do) and the divine name יָהּ (Yah), a short form of the name of God. This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common in Israel and expressed the parents' trust in God's action.
H4641Z.emploi: Maaséja appears only once in the Bible, mentioned in Jeremiah 35:4. He is identified as the son of Shallum and holds the title of 'gatekeeper' (שׁמֵר הַסַּף), an important function at the temple in Jerusalem. This brief but precise mention situates him as an official character of the temple during the time of the prophet Jeremiah, in the final days of the kingdom of Judah before the Babylonian exile.

sens: Capitale de la Basse-Égypte, ville majeure du Nil
H4644.detail: 1. Moph is a large city in Egypt, the capital of Lower Egypt, located on the western bank of the Nile, about 15 kilometers south of present-day Cairo. It was a major political and religious center of ancient Egypt. In Hosea 9:6, the prophet mentions Moph as a place where the deported Israelites will find graves, highlighting death and exile far from their promised land.
H4644.origine: The Hebrew name מֹף (Moph) or נֹף (Noph) refers to the Egyptian city that the Greeks called Memphis. Its name would literally mean "haven of the good" in ancient Egyptian, reflecting its importance as a major port and commercial center on the Nile.
H4644.emploi: Moph appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Hosea 9:6. The prophet Hosea uses it to evoke the tragic fate of unfaithful Israelites: driven from their land, they will perish in Egypt and be buried in Moph. This proper name represents here exile, death far from the homeland, and divine judgment on the rebellious people. The context is one of prophetic threats addressed to the kingdoms of Israel.
H4644.portee: For the biblical reader, Moph symbolizes the terrible consequence of unfaithfulness: exile in a foreign land and death far from divine blessing. Hosea reminds us that abandoning God leads to dispersion and perdition, while returning to the Lord alone offers life and restoration.

sens: Ce sur quoi on tire, ce qu'on vise
Point faible, victime facile
Objet d'attaque ou d'hostilité
H4645.detail:
1. The word literally designates what one aims at with a weapon, the target of an arrow or a blow — like a shooting target. Job exclaims that he has become the target of God's arrows, as if God were using him for target practice (Job 7:20).
2. By extension, it means being exposed, defenseless, the weak point on which one is focused. Job complains of being made a target, meaning he is left unprotected against the blows of the Lord.
3. More broadly, it is the object of an attack, of hostility, the goal aimed at by one who seeks to harm or dominate.
H4645.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to strike," "to reach." The form "miphgâ" is a noun that designates what is touched, struck — the result of the action of striking. It is a rarely used word in the Bible, as if the context of Job (the suffering of the afflicted righteous) called for this precise image: the target of an attack.
H4645.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 7:20. Job uses it to express his confusion and pain: he wonders what evil he has done to God to become His target, to endure His endless blows. The image is that of a defenseless man, repeatedly aimed at, unable to understand why he has become the object of this divine hostility. It is a typical cry of distress from the book of Job.
H4645.portee: This word helps the reader grasp the depth of Job's suffering: he does not see himself as a punished sinner, but as a target subjected to an incomprehensible attack. For the Christian, this reminds us that the suffering of the innocent raises a real question of faith, and that Job refuses to easily justify God without understanding. It is an invitation to spiritual honesty before the mystery of pain.

sens: The last breath, the expiration of life
The definitive absence of life, the end of existence
H4646.detail:
1. The word describes the moment when life extinguishes: it is the final breath that escapes the body, as when one gives up the ghost. In Job 11:20, the wicked see their "death" as the only refuge left to them, meaning they come to wish for this ultimate expiration, this end of everything.
2. More broadly, it designates the state of death itself, the definitive deprivation of life. It is the total absence toward which the wicked turn due to a lack of true hope.
H4646.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to blow" or "to breathe." It is constructed as an action noun: mapp-ach literally describes "the action of blowing" or "the expiration." This image of breath is at the heart of the Hebrew understanding of life: everything that breathes lives, and when the breath stops, death occurs. Life itself is often called "breath" or "spirit" in the Bible.
H4646.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 11:20. Zophar, one of Job's friends, states that the wicked have no refuge except death itself. The context shows men without true hope, for whom death paradoxically becomes their only expectation. It is a rare and poetic word, chosen to emphasize the total absence of consolation in the face of divine judgment.
H4646.portee: This passage reminds the Christian reader that living without God and without hope leads to an existential dead end. Death, far from being a deliverance for one who rejects God, becomes a threat without redemption. Conversely, the Christian hope in resurrection radically transforms our relationship with death.

sens: Instrument for blowing air onto a fire
Air blown forcefully to revive or control a flame
That which kindles, heats, and ignites
H4647.detail:
1. The bellows is a tool that blacksmiths and metallurgists use to force air into a hearth, in order to revive the fire and make it hot enough to work with metals. In Jeremiah 6:29, the prophet describes a "burning" bellows that cannot even properly melt the corrupt metal of Israel: the image is of this primitive bellows, inflated and deflated continuously to feed the embers.
2. The word also evokes the action itself: blowing air, forcefully chasing away wind. It is a useful gesture to stoke a weak fire or transform it into a furnace capable of melting metal.
3. Figuratively, the bellows represents that which ignites, that which provokes or exacerbates a situation. Here, the prophet's image suggests that even the most energetic efforts cannot purify what has become intrinsically corrupt.
H4647.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of "to blow" or "to inflate." The bellows itself is named after this action: it is the tool that allows one to "puff," to apply pressure. This instrument was known throughout the ancient Levant for metallurgy and forging.
H4647.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 6:29. The prophet uses it in a vision of judgment against Jerusalem and Judah: despite all the efforts of the bellows — in other words, all the calls of the prophet and the trials that God sends to purify His people — the metal refuses to melt, the dross does not detach. The image expresses the hardening of the heart: no fire, even if continuously revived, can transform what has hardened in sin.
H4647.portee: This image of the unsuccessful bellows teaches the reader the seriousness of spiritual hardening. It shows that the power of God (represented by the bellows that ignites) can be rejected by a people or a person who refuses to be transformed. It is a call not to ignore God's efforts to purify us and bring us back to Him.

sens: Grandson of Saul and son of Jonathan
Son of Rizpah and grandson of Saul
H4648G.detail: Mephibosheth primarily refers to a character from the tribe of Benjamin: the son of Jonathan and grandson of King Saul (2 Samuel 4:4). He became lame at the age of five while fleeing after the death of Saul and Jonathan, and he lived in hiding until David sought him out to show him kindness. David restored Saul's lands to him and welcomed him to his royal table (2 Samuel 9:10). The name also refers to another Mephibosheth, son of Rizpah (a concubine of Saul) and brother of Armoni, who was delivered to the Gibeonites along with his brother to be executed in order to atone for the injustice that Saul had committed (2 Samuel 21:7-8).
H4648G.origine: The Hebrew name means "exterminates the idol" or "shame of the master," composed of roots evoking destruction and idol. In 1 Chronicles 8:34 and 9:40, the same son of Jonathan is called Merib-Baal, an alternative name that underscores the same historical realities. These names reflect the beliefs and circumstances of the families of Benjamin during the time of the united monarchy.
H4648G.emploi: Mephibosheth appears mainly in the story of David in 2 Samuel. The most well-known is the son of Jonathan (2 Samuel 4:4; 9:6-13), who embodies David's grace toward the descendants of Saul despite past rivalry. David seeks him out, treats him with honor, and feeds him at his table despite his infirmity (2 Samuel 9:10-13). During David's flight from Absalom, Ziba, Mephibosheth's servant, abandons him (2 Samuel 16:1-4), but after the king's triumphant return, Mephibosheth explains that he could not follow the king due to his lameness (2 Samuel 19:24-30). Another Mephibosheth, son of Rizpah, is mentioned in 2 Samuel 21:7-8 as one of the victims delivered to the Gibeonites.
H4648G.portee: The story of Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan, illustrates free grace: David honors and supports him not because he has earned it, but out of kindness toward the son of his friend Jonathan. His infirmity makes him dependent on the king's compassion, a poignant image of one who receives favor without having earned it. It is a biblical reflection of divine grace that extends to one who can do nothing to earn it.

sens: Son of Saul and Rizpah, delivered to the Gibeonites
H4648H.detail: 1. Mephibosheth is a son of Saul, the first king of Israel, born of Rizpah, a concubine of Saul. Along with his brother Armoni, he is mentioned during a grave event: King David delivers them to the Gibeonites to atone for a fault of Saul and to stop a famine that strikes the land (2 Samuel 21:8). He is a marginal character in biblical history, not glorious, caught in the consequences of the sins of a previous generation.
H4648H.origine: The Hebrew name מְפִיבֹשֶׁת means "he who exterminates the idol" or "who destroys the idol." It reflects a religious intent of the parents: to reject idols and affirm faith in God alone. This name belongs to the royal family of Saul, a house marked by spiritual and political tensions in Israel's history.
H4648H.emploi: Mephibosheth is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 21:8, in the context of a famine that lasted three years during David's reign. David seeks to know the cause and learns that it is due to a broken oath that Saul made to the Gibeonites. To rectify this injustice, David asks the Gibeonites what he can do. They demand seven descendants of Saul. David therefore delivers Mephibosheth and his brother Armoni, along with five other grandsons of Saul born of Merab. These seven men are executed by the Gibeonites, and their bodies are hung on a mountain.
H4648H.portee: This account reminds us that the sins of one generation can affect subsequent generations, and that divine justice requires restitution. Mephibosheth, innocent of Saul's crime, pays with his life a debt he did not incur. It is a call to the seriousness of the broken oath before God and the consequences of evil that reverberate beyond the one who committed it.

sens: Son of Benjamin
Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of Egypt and the desert
H4649.detail: Muppim is one of the sons of Benjamin, the twelfth son of Jacob. He is mentioned in Genesis 46:21 among the descendants of Benjamin who came to Egypt with Jacob. His name literally means "serpent," but it simply designates this member of the patriarchal family. In later texts (Numbers 26:39 and 1 Chronicles 8:5), he is also called Shupham or Shephuphan, which shows that biblical genealogies can present variations of names according to the lists.
H4649.origine: The name Muppim means "serpent" in Hebrew, derived from the verb יפף which evokes the hissing or image of a serpent. This name belongs to the family of names from the second generation of Jacob's children, who were born before the descent into Egypt.
H4649.emploi: Muppim is mentioned only once as such, in Genesis 46:21, in the list of the sons of Benjamin who accompany Jacob to Egypt. However, he reappears under the variants Shupham (Numbers 26:39) and Shephuphan (1 Chronicles 8:5), indicating that this character has a place in the genealogies of the people of Israel, particularly in the tribe of Benjamin. These genealogical lists serve to establish lineage and territorial inheritance at the time of the distribution of the lands of Canaan.

sens: a weapon made of a thick, heavy stick, often studded with spikes or knobs
figuratively, something that strikes and wounds like a club
H4650.detail:
1. A club is a formidable weapon used in warfare: a heavy, thick stick, sometimes studded with spikes or knots, wielded to strike the enemy with force. It was a common weapon in ancient combat, terrifying due to its destructive power.
2. The word is also used figuratively to describe something that deeply wounds like a violent physical blow. In Proverbs 25:18, false testimony is compared to a club among other weapons: it is a treacherous and devastating blow that destroys the reputation and life of the one against whom testimony is borne.
H4650.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to scatter" or "to disperse" — the image evokes the devastating effect of a club that scatters everything in its path. It is a weapon of dispersion and massive destruction, unlike a sword or arrow that strikes more precisely.
H4650.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 25:18. In this passage, false testimony is listed among the most dangerous weapons: the club (false testimony), the sword, and the sharp arrow. This enumeration shows that a lying word is as destructive as a physical weapon. The context of Proverbs, which are teachings of wisdom, emphasizes the devastating power of the word: a judicial lie ruins the one it targets.
H4650.portee: The text reminds us that our words, especially false accusations, are weapons as deadly as material arms. Accusing someone unjustly is not a mere mistake: it is a violent blow to their life, family, and reputation. This passage calls each one to responsibility in speech and to truth, especially before justice.

sens: The debris, dust, or residues that fall during the sifting or screening of grain
The scraps or hanging parts of a creature
Figuratively: what is contemptible, worthless, thrown away
H4651.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the refuse of grain after sifting — the fine dust, chaff, small fragments that are eliminated to keep the wheat pure. In Amos 8:6, dishonest merchants are ready to sell even the "sifting of wheat," meaning the most contemptible remains, for profit: the image shows how they exploit even the poorest.
2. The word also describes scraps or parts that hang and detach — notably the scales and folds of skin of the crocodile in Job 41:14, where the text speaks of the "fleshy parts" that hold together on the monster. It is an image of what is loose, flapping, in contrast to solidity.
3. By extension, it means anything that is rejected, worthless, fallen into contempt — a poetic term to express abjection and uselessness.
H4651.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to fall" or "to tumble" — hence the image of what falls, tumbles, or detaches. Words of the same family speak of falling, ruin, destruction. The primary image is that of particles that crumbled from the grain during winnowing or sifting: what crumbles is precisely what is rejected.
H4651.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible. In Job 41:14, it describes the hanging fleshy parts of the crocodile — a detail of the monstrous portrait of Leviathan, a creature of brute power. In Amos 8:6, it symbolizes the moral degradation of the poor, reduced to the condition of "sifting": unscrupulous merchants are ready to sell them as one sells the worthless residues of grain. In both cases, the word paints a reality of rejection or degradation.
H4651.portee: This word awakens the believer's conscience on two points. First, it warns against the greed for gain that dehumanizes the poor and treats them as debris: this is the lesson of the passage from Amos. Secondly, it invites contemplation of God's hidden order: in creation, even the refuse of grain has its place and role. Nothing is truly waste in the eyes of the Creator.

sens: An extraordinary work that astonishes and amazes
A superhuman act that surpasses human understanding
A striking manifestation of God's power
H4652.detail:
1. A wonder is a work that strikes by its extraordinary and sublime nature, evoking admiration and astonishment. In Job 37:16, the text speaks of the "wonders" of the Most High, these delicate balances of the clouds that only perfect knowledge can orchestrate: it is the image of a work so refined and powerful that it surpasses our understanding.
2. This word designates an act that reveals superhuman power, something that man cannot conceive or accomplish by his own strength. The wonders of God in nature — the play of the clouds, the movements of the sky — demonstrate absolute intelligence and mastery.
3. In a spiritual sense, a wonder is a manifestation of God's infinite glory and wisdom, something that elevates the soul towards wonder and worship.
H4652.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root evoking the idea of "to make a wonder" or "to accomplish the extraordinary." It is a term that expresses superhuman action, a work that fascinates because it reveals transcendent power. The word is formed to emphasize the astonishing and divine character of what is accomplished.
H4652.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 37:16. It is used in a context of cosmic contemplation: Elihu, Job's friend, questions him about his understanding of the workings of the clouds and the wonders of the one whose knowledge is perfect, namely God. The context emphasizes human inability to comprehend divine works, and the wonder as a sign of absolute wisdom that surpasses created reason.
H4652.portee: Meditating on the wonders of God invites the believer to recognize his inability to penetrate the secrets of creation and to place his trust in the one whose knowledge and power are limitless. It is a call to humility before God and to worshipful wonder at His work.

sens: Organized group of people assigned a specific function
Distribution into several distinct groups
H4653.detail:
1. The word designates a group of people — notably priests — assigned to a specific task or service. In 2 Chronicles 35:12, it refers to the "different" ancestral houses, meaning the distinct families of the people, each responsible for bringing their offerings.
2. More broadly, it expresses the idea of distribution or classification: dividing a whole into organized sections, each having its own role. It is a way of ordering and structuring.
H4653.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to separate" or "to divide." It expresses the action of creating distinctions, sharing something into different portions, each complete and autonomous. This image of ordered separation is at the heart of the meaning: not a simple rupture, but a thoughtful organization.
H4653.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (2 Chronicles 35:12), in the context of a great Passover celebrated under King Josiah. There, it designates the different families of the people, each forming a distinct unit to present their burnt offerings. The term emphasizes that the temple service was organized methodically, in groups or categories that cooperated in worship.
H4653.portee: This word reminds us that God loves order and organization in worship and community. Each group, each family has its place and responsibility. It is an invitation to recognize that serving the Lord is not chaos, but a harmony where everyone contributes according to their part.

sens: Complete destruction of a city or building
Debris and rubble of a collapsed structure
State of devastation and material ruin
Figuratively, moral or spiritual destruction of a person
H4654A.detail: 1. A ruin is primarily the total destruction of a city or a structure: in Isaiah 17:1, Damascus, the great capital, will be reduced to "a heap of ruins" on the day of judgment. 2. The word then designates the visible debris and rubble: everything that remains of a ravaged city, scattered stones and collapsed walls. 3. It is the state of material devastation: a ruin embodies complete collapse, when nothing remains. 4. By extension, the Bible uses this word to describe the spiritual or moral destruction of a person or a people: when sin or God's judgment destroys everything.
H4654A.origine: The Hebrew word mappalah comes from the root "nasaph" (to fall, to collapse), conjugated to express the state of what has fallen. It is a variant of mapelah (מַפֵּלָה), with the same meaning. It is a feminine noun designating an event (the fall, the destruction) or its visible result (the ruins). The word evokes the concrete image of collapse: walls that crumble, a city that is annihilated.
H4654A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 17:1, in a prophecy against Damascus. Isaiah announces that the proud Syrian capital will become a mere "heap of ruins." This is in a context of divine judgment: God destroys rebellious and idolatrous cities to punish the pride of nations. The word serves to show total collapse, the annihilation of what seemed powerful and unshakeable.
H4654A.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality of God's judgment on nations that refuse His law. Seeing a great city reduced to ruins concretely illustrates the vanity of human powers and the inevitability of divine justice. For the believer, it is an invitation to seek security, not in earthly fortifications, but in a relationship with God.

sens: Debris of a collapsed structure
Remains of a destroyed city or fortress
Destruction, annihilation of a power
H4654B.detail:
1. A ruin is primarily what remains of a building or fortification when it has collapsed or been destroyed: debris of stone, fallen walls, toppled towers. In Isaiah 23:13, the Lord speaks of the palaces of Tyre that the Chaldeans have overturned, turning them into ruins.
2. The word then designates the state of an entire ravaged city: no longer an isolated house, but a whole city reduced to a heap of stones. Isaiah 25:2 gives the most striking image: "The strong city into a heap of ruins," showing the complete annihilation of a capital.
3. Figuratively, ruin means the collapse of a power, the end of a domination that seemed unshakeable: glorious Tyre and its barbaric fortifications become dust, never to be rebuilt.
H4654B.origine: The Hebrew word מַפֵּלָה (mappelah) comes from the root נָפַל (naphal), which means "to fall," "to collapse." A ruin is what has fallen: the result of the fall. This root is rich in images: the fall of a tower, the fall of a king, the fall of a people. The word expresses both the action (to fall) and its lasting result (to remain destroyed).
H4654B.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in the prophet Isaiah, who announces the destruction of great powers. In Isaiah 23:13, he speaks of Tyre ravaged by the Assyrians and Chaldeans. In Isaiah 25:2, the prophet praises the Lord for having brought down a strong city into ruins. In both contexts, ruin designates not only the physical state of a destroyed city but also God's judgment that brings down human powers. It is a word of prophetic judgment.
H4654B.portee: This word reminds the believer that human fortresses, even the most glorious like Tyre, are nothing before the will of God. No earthly power is unshakeable. This reassures the fearful: tyrannical empires will fall. It also teaches humility: to build without God is to build on a foundation that will collapse.

sens: Means or way to escape from danger
Hasty flight
H4655.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the means or place by which one can escape, the possibility of fleeing from peril. In Psalm 55:9, the psalmist wishes for a quick "escape": he wants to flee in haste, faster than the wind or the storm, to escape the tumult of his enemies. It is the concrete image of fleeing away from danger.
2. By extension, the word can designate the very act of escaping, the hasty and urgent flight. The escape is not a slow withdrawal, but a hurried departure, driven by fear or necessity.
H4655.origine: The Hebrew word miph.lat comes from a root that means "to escape, to flee." It is built on the verb "palat," which evokes the rapid movement of one fleeing from danger. The family of this root includes other words related to flight and deliverance. It is a word that carries within it the urgency and speed of the fugitive.
H4655.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalm 55:9. The psalmist, overwhelmed by the threats surrounding him, seeks an escape — a way to flee quickly and safely. The context shows a man in distress, pressed by enemies and plots, who dreams of being able to fly far away from this tumult. It is a prayer for quick and effective deliverance.
H4655.portee: This word reminds the reader that in the face of danger and distress, fleeing is not always cowardice: it is sometimes wisdom. The psalmist teaches us that it is legitimate to seek an escape when one is persecuted or threatened. It also encourages trust in God, who offers protection and deliverance to those who seek Him in trial.

sens: Object of horrible and abominable worship, carved image of a deity
Repugnant thing that provokes horror and disgust
H4656.detail:
1. The word designates an object of worship, generally a statue or a carved image, that is adored as a god — but with a connotation of abomination and horror. In 1 Kings 15:13, the queen mother Maacah made an idol for Ashtoreth, the goddess of fertility; King Asa tore it down and burned it, thereby showing his radical rejection of this abomination.
2. More broadly, the word expresses the moral and religious repulsion that such a thing inspires: it is not simply a statue, but something horrible, filthy, that evokes disgust. Maacah's act was not innocent: it was a worship that was completely abominable in the eyes of God.
H4656.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of causing fear, repulsion, or horror. The original image is that of the shudder, the recoil of horror one feels in front of something repugnant. This is why it is not merely a sculpted image, but something marked by the seal of abomination and impurity.
H4656.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, in two very close parallel accounts (1 Kings 15:13 and 2 Chronicles 15:16). It describes the idol that Queen Mother Maacah dedicated to the goddess Ashtoreth. In both cases, the context shows an act of complete and voluntary destruction: Asa does not merely remove it; he burns it. This rather rare vocabulary emphasizes the dimension of horror and abomination that idolatry represents, in the eyes of biblical faith.
H4656.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that idolatry is not a neutral issue or a religious option among others: it is something horrible and abominable in the eyes of God. The example of Asa, who completely destroys his own mother's idol, shows that faithfulness to God requires the courage to radically reject what contradicts Him, even when it is personally costly.

sens: oscillating movement from side to side
unstable or suspended balance
H4657.detail:
1. Sway refers to the regular movement by which something oscillates, balancing from side to side around a central point — like a branch swaying in the wind or a suspended object moving. In Job 37:16, Eliphaz speaks of the "sway of the clouds": the image of clouds floating, moving freely in the sky under the action of forces that God perfectly controls.

2. The word also describes more broadly the subtle balance, the state of delicate stability that depends on forces in tension. The clouds maintain their place; they do not fall, suspended in this balance that only the "perfect knowledge" of the Creator can maintain.
H4657.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of swaying, weighing, holding in balance — the same family as that of weight and scale, an instrument that measures by balancing two plates. Hebrew often describes invisible or abstract realities through images of weight and movement: here, the cosmic balance of the created world.
H4657.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (in Job 37:16). It is used by Eliphaz in his final speech to Job to express admiration for the wonders of creation — notably the clouds that remain suspended in the sky, neither falling nor flying away. It is a poetic term that emphasizes how all of nature manifests the order and wisdom of God: everything has its balance, its assigned place.
H4657.portee: Meditating on this sway of the clouds invites the Christian to recognize that the entire universe — even the most imperceptible phenomena — rests on the wisdom and power of God. Nothing is left to chance: even what seems to float freely obeys an invisible divine order. It is an invitation to trust the One who maintains all things in balance.

sens: Corpse of an animal or a person
Destruction of a city or a power
Collapse of a structure
Disastrous consequence of someone's fall
H4658.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the dead body of an animal: in Judges 14:8, Samson sees the corpse of the lion he killed and finds honey formed in its body. This is the most concrete and closest image to the literal sense.

2. It extends to the complete ruin of a city or a power: in Ezekiel 26:15 and 26:18, it speaks of the fall (destruction) of Tyre, a powerful city, whose surrounding islands tremble upon hearing of the disaster. The word then depicts the collapse of greatness.

3. It describes the collapse of a structure or an established reality: in Ezekiel 31:13, after the fall of the tree (the kingdom of Egypt), the birds of the sky settle on the debris and the animals nest among the fallen branches. The image is one of total destruction.

4. The word also evokes the visible and terrible consequences that follow the fall: in Proverbs 29:16, the righteous will behold the fall of the wicked, meaning the moment when their power and prosperity collapse, the fruit of their sin.
H4658.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to fall" or "to drop." The form נפל (napal) expresses the action of falling; mappélet is its nominal form that designates what has fallen or the state of what has collapsed. The word always paints a spectacular fall and a state of ruin or death that results from it.
H4658.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the prophetic books (notably Ezekiel). In Judges 14:8, it literally means the corpse of the lion. But most of its uses (Ezekiel 26-32, Proverbs 29) speak of the fall of kingdoms or powers: Tyre appears several times. The context is always one of great and visible destruction, often accompanied by mourning and fear. The word emphasizes less the action of falling than the state of devastation that remains after the fall.
H4658.portee: This word reminds us that human power, even that of great kingdoms, is fragile and subject to collapse. For the believing reader, the fall of the wicked and the enemies of God is not a distant rumor: it is a historical reality that the righteous will behold. It invites us not to place our trust in empires or earthly riches, but in divine justice.

sens: product of labor, something made by hand
action, completed work
creation, realization of intellect or art
H4659A.detail:
1. The word primarily designates an object, a concrete product that is manufactured or created: it is the visible result of work. In Proverbs 8:22, Wisdom itself is called a "work" of the Lord, as if it were the first object that God shaped before all creation — it is His first production, His masterpiece.
2. The word can also refer to the action or activity itself: it is the work in progress, the effort being accomplished.
3. Finally, it can refer to a more immaterial realization, the visible expression of an intention or wisdom — what shows the genius of the one who conceived it.
H4659A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to do, to make." It etymologically designates what is "done," the product of action. It is a noun formed to express the result of work: there are several words in the Old Testament from the same family that all refer to the idea of doing, creating, or working.
H4659A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible: in Proverbs 8:22, in the discourse of Wisdom presenting itself. There it asserts that the Lord created her "the first of His works," which emphasizes her antiquity and unique importance. The choice of the word "work" rather than a simple "creation" highlights the concrete and intentional nature of her origin: she is not merely an attribute of God, but a true production of His hand, prior to all things.
H4659A.portee: This passage invites the believer to recognize Wisdom as a presence of God intimately linked to His creation: it is not an abstract concept, but a living reality, the fruit of God's creative work. For one who meditates on these verses, understanding that Wisdom is God's first work is to grasp that it presides over the entire universe and is the way through which God establishes order in the world.

sens: Action, concrete realization of a person
Powerful or remarkable act
In particular, action manifesting the power of God
H4659B.detail:
1. The word designates an action that one performs, a work that one accomplishes, a visible and concrete realization — what someone does with their hands or by their power. It is the act performed, the visible result of an activity.
2. It often emphasizes the remarkable or powerful nature of this action: an act that manifests strength, authority, greatness. In Psalms 46:9, the "works" of the Lord are the devastations He has wrought on the earth, His spectacular interventions.
3. In the Bible, the word particularly applies to the actions of God that reveal His power and majesty. In Psalms 66:5, we are invited to contemplate the "works of God": His actions that make Him fearsome and that manifest His authority over mankind.
H4659B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to do, to act, to accomplish." It is formed with a prefix that indicates action or concrete realization. It is a noun that simply names what is done: the work as the fruit of an activity, whether human or divine. The root evokes the idea of work done and visible results.
H4659B.emploi: The word appears twice in the Psalms, in liturgical and contemplative contexts. In Psalms 46:9, the "works" refer to the Lord's interventions in history, particularly His acts of warfare and His fearsome judgments on the earth. In Psalms 66:5, in the same context: we are called to contemplate the "works of God" as a sign of His fearfulness and power over humanity. Both occurrences invite the reader to recognize in God's acts a manifestation of His greatness and authority.
H4659B.portee: This word invites the believer not to remain blind to God's interventions in the world and in history. Observing the works of God is learning to recognize His power, to fear His majesty, and to give Him glory. For the psalmist, contemplating these acts is not an intellectual exercise, but an act of worship: it is seeing God at work and responding with reverence.

sens: Instrument that destroys or breaks
Weapon intended to sow devastation
H4660.detail:
1. The word designates an instrument of destruction, particularly a weapon. In Ezekiel's vision, the six men arrive "each with his instrument of destruction in hand" (Ezekiel 9:2): these instruments are the tools of divine judgment on Jerusalem, intended to strike and devastate.
2. By extension, the word evokes the action of devastating, of sowing ruin. It is the effect produced by this instrument: massive and complete destruction.
H4660.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to break," "to shatter." It is formed to specifically designate the object that breaks or destroys — in this case, a weapon of war. This root evokes the image of a violent force that pulverizes or annihilates its target.
H4660.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 9:2, where it designates the instruments of destruction held by the six men in the apocalyptic vision of judgment on Jerusalem. In this context, these instruments are not precisely named (swords, axes, or others): the text emphasizes their function — to destroy — rather than their form. It is a rare and particularly grave term, used to accentuate the solemnity of divine judgment.
H4660.portee: This passage shows that God's judgment is real and armed. The faithful who take refuge in prayer see that God acts concretely against evil and idolatry. For the believer, this reminds us that indifference toward God does not escape His attention, and that His judgment is executed with inexorable force.

sens: Tool or weapon with a heavy head and short handle, used for striking and breaking
Figuratively, instrument of divine or human destruction
H4661.detail:
1. A hammer is a tool or weapon characterized by a massive head and a short handle, designed to strike with force and break. It is a concrete object of daily life, used for both work and war. In Jeremiah 51:20, God calls Nebuchadnezzar His "hammer": it is a raw image that underscores the striking power and capacity to destroy.
2. Figuratively, the hammer designates an instrument or agent of large-scale destruction. God uses this comparison to express how a people or a king can become the tool of His will, breaking and crushing other nations with the force of a hammer blow. This image evokes the inevitability and controlled violence of divine judgment.
H4661.origine: The Hebrew word מַפֵּץ (mappets) derives from a root meaning "to break," "to burst," or "to scatter." It is a concrete word, formed from the verb פּוץ (putz) which expresses the action of scattering or fragmenting. The image of the hammer or mallet naturally comes from this idea of shattering: it is the tool that strikes and breaks.
H4661.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 51:20. In this passage of judgment against Babylon, God addresses Nebuchadnezzar and describes him as a hammer, a weapon of war by which He breaks nations and destroys kingdoms. The usage is clearly metaphorical and theological: the hammer is not a mere object, but a symbol of divine judgment executed by human power. This unique occurrence is sufficient to show the symbolic importance of the word in the Old Testament.
H4661.portee: This verse reminds us of a difficult but biblical truth: God controls history and uses the powers of this world, even the most brutal, to accomplish His purposes. The hammer, an image of blind and destructive force, becomes in God's hand an instrument of justice. This invites the believer to recognize that God remains sovereign, even over empires that seem invincible, and that all human judgment ultimately remains subject to His will.

sens: Guard post or designated place for roll call
Gate of a city intended for troop review
H4662G.detail:
1. The word designates the post or station where roll call and gathering take place — it is the assigned place for counting and inspecting. In Nehemiah 3:31, it refers to the Gate of Muster, an entrance to Jerusalem where troops or contingents were to gather for inspection.
2. By extension, the word can also refer to the inspection itself or the action of roll call, as the place and the action are linked.
H4662G.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to assign, to designate, to count." It is formed with the prefix "mi-" ("from, since") and a base element related to the idea of counting and organizing. It is an administrative and military term: it describes the organization of gathering and oversight.
H4662G.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Nehemiah 3:31, where it designates the Gate of Muster of Jerusalem during the reconstruction of its walls after the exile. It is a specialized term, related to the military and administrative context of the fortified city.
H4662G.portee: This name of the gate reminds us that restored Jerusalem was a fortified and organized city, capable of defending itself. It evokes the order and discipline that God establishes in the return of His people: not a chaotic return, but a structured reconstruction, with its burdens and responsibilities.

sens: Action of counting and recording a population
Order given to accomplish a task or function
Designated place or location for a specific activity
H4662H.detail:
1. Counting is the action of counting people, particularly warriors or the populace. In 2 Samuel 24:9 and 1 Chronicles 21:5, the word refers to the role or record of the counting of the people: Joab reports to the king the exact total of men able to bear arms in Israel and Judah.
2. The word can also mean an order or instruction given to direct work. In 2 Chronicles 31:13, several Levites work "according to the order of King Hezekiah": the word here denotes the instruction or directive that frames their service in the house of God.
3. Finally, the word designates a place or location reserved for an activity. In Ezekiel 43:21, it refers to the "designated place" outside the sanctuary where the sin offering is to be burned.
H4662H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to place," "to fix," or "to establish." The word "miph'qad" (מִפְקָד) is a noun formed from this root and primarily denotes a "designated place" or an "assigned post"; from there, the meanings of "counting" (enumeration of people at a given place) and "order" (instruction that fixes a task or location) arise.
H4662H.emploi: This word appears four times in the Old Testament. The first two occurrences (2 Samuel 24:9 and 1 Chronicles 21:5) concern the counting of the people ordered by King David and carried out by Joab: it refers to the register or role that enumerates the men of fighting age. The third (2 Chronicles 31:13) uses it for the order or directive given by King Hezekiah regarding the organization of worship. The fourth (Ezekiel 43:21) designates it as a space or location specifically reserved for burning a sacrifice. Thus, the word denotes realities that share the commonality of being "established" or "fixed": an official enumeration, a given instruction, or a determined place.
H4662H.portee: This word reminds us that a well-ordered communion or community relies on clarity: counting those who are part of it, knowing the number and identity of each, issuing clear orders, and defining places and roles. For the people of Israel and for the Church, this organization reflects God's concern for His people and His desire that everything be done "decently and in order."

sens: Place on the shore where ships can shelter and unload their cargo
Stopping and resting place for a boat or crew
H4664.detail:
1. A port is a cove or natural bay on the coast where ships find refuge and can anchor. It is the place of arrival and departure for ships, where goods can be loaded and unloaded safely. In the Song of Deborah, Asher settled at the ports: this means that his tribe established itself near the good anchorages of the Mediterranean, in an ideal position for maritime trade.
2. By extension, it is a place where one finds rest and security. A port offers the ship and its crew a pause, a shelter against storms and the perils of the sea. This image of refuge and tranquility well summarizes what a port represents for the traveler: a haven in the storm.
H4664.origine: The Hebrew word מִפְרָץ (miphratz) comes from the root פרץ (pharatz), which means "to break through" or "to open" — the idea of a breach, an opening in the coast. A port is literally a "natural opening" of the shore where the waters carve out and allow ships to enter. The prefix מִ (mi) indicates the place or location, hence "open passage place." This root evokes the image of a coast that opens up to welcome the ship.
H4664.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the Song of Deborah (Judges 5:17). In this context, it describes the coastal ports where the tribe of Asher settled. The Song enumerates the military role of each tribe during the victory over Sisera: Asher, unlike Gilead, Reuben, and Dan, chose to remain in its maritime ports, suggesting that its coastal geography gave it a commercial and defensive vocation related to the sea rather than a warrior one in the interior.
H4664.portee: This word reminds us that in God's plan, each tribe of Israel received its own territory and vocation. Asher was established near the sea to prosper through trade and coastal defense, not for mountain warfare. This shows us that God uses our position and natural resources to call us to a particular service. Accepting our "place" also means accepting our limits and finding our peace in what God has planned.

sens: the back and lower part of the neck, where it articulates with the shoulders
by extension, the nape considered as the most vulnerable point of the body
H4665.detail:
1. The nape is the part of the neck located at the back, at the junction with the shoulders — the point where the head connects to the rest of the body. It is a fragile and vulnerable area. In 1 Samuel 4:18, when the old priest Eli falls backward from his seat, it is his nape that breaks: the word precisely describes this fracture of the neck that leads to his death.
2. Figuratively, the nape can evoke the vulnerability of one who is dominated or struck down — it is in some way the ultimate weak point. Although only this passage from 1 Samuel uses this word in biblical Hebrew, the image of the broken nape remains symbolically that of a definitive defeat and an irreversible fall.
H4665.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to articulate" or "to join": the nape is the joint, the articulation that connects the head to the body. It belongs to the family of words designating the joints and connections of the human body.
H4665.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in 1 Samuel 4:18. It is a rather rare word, which emphasizes the precise anatomy of the breaking point. The context is dramatic: Eli, the high priest of Israel, learns of the arrival of the Philistines and the capture of the Ark of God. In shock and at his old age, he falls from his seat and breaks his nape — an anatomical detail that underscores that his death is not merely an end, but a concrete physical fall.
H4665.portee: This word reminds us of the fragility of the human body, even that of the great and the aged. For the biblical reader, Eli's death, described with this anatomical detail, shows that no one escapes the consequences of their actions or the unfolding of events: age and prestige do not protect against God's judgment.

sens: action of spreading out, of deploying
thing deployed, spread out (fabric, sail)
H4666.detail:
1. The word evokes the action of deploying, of spreading something out. In Job 36:29, it refers to the deployment of clouds in the sky: "Who can understand the deployment of the cloud," meaning the way they spread and develop in space.
2. By extension, it designates the deployed object itself, the thing that is spread out. In Ezekiel 27:7, the word describes the sails and curtains of the ship of Tyre, these magnificent fabrics spread out for navigation and adorning the boat.
